articles.title_orig: Israel Election Live Updates: Record Voter Turnout as Netanyahu Faces Challenge Led by Eisenkot
articles.title_zh: Israel Election Live Updates: Record Voter Turnout as Netanyahu Faces Challenge Led by Eisenkot
articles.content_orig:
Jerusalem 8:13 p.m. Oct. 27
Aaron Boxerman David M. Halbfinger and Leo Sands
Israelis flocked to the polls in record numbers on Tuesday in what is widely seen as the most consequential election in the country’s history, as voters decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition in power or chart a new course.
By 6 p.m. local time (12 p.m. Eastern), four hours before polls were scheduled to close, 66.7 percent of voters had cast ballots.
Turnout appeared to be particularly high, compared with previous elections, among Arab citizens, who make up about a fifth of Israel’s population. By late afternoon, hours before the polls were set to close, turnout in some Arab-majority towns had exceeded the totals from the last election, in 2022.
Responding to the high turnout in those towns, Mr. Netanyahu accused Arab citizens of “trying to steal the elections,” repeatedly using brazen and overtly racial appeals to push his right-wing base to vote.
The election is Israel’s first since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, upended the nation and ignited three years of war.
Voters have a choice between two blocs offering starkly different visions. Mr. Netanyahu is seeking re-election at the helm of the most far-right government in Israeli history. His coalition of nationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jews faces an ideologically diverse group of Jewish opposition parties loosely led by Gadi Eisenkot , a former military chief of staff whose son was killed in the Gaza war. Parties representing Arab citizens of Israel also staunchly oppose Mr. Netanyahu’s government.
Both sides are framing the election as a make-or-break moment for the country. Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition offers the promise of a more religious Israel with an ever-tighter grip over the West Bank and Gaza. His opponents are casting the vote as the last chance to preserve democracy and pull Israel back from the brink of becoming a pariah state under international sanctions.
Voting will close at 10 p.m. but is unlikely to deliver an immediate verdict on who will be the next prime minister. Opinion polls suggest that Mr. Netanyahu’s allies and rivals are roughly tied, and assembling a governing coalition in Israel’s parliamentary system could take weeks or months .
Opposition leaders led by Mr. Eisenkot have called for a reckoning over what they call Mr. Netanyahu’s failure to prevent the catastrophic Oct. 7 attacks. They also have pledged to repair Israel’s shattered image abroad , including by cracking down on Israeli extremist violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Mr. Netanyahu has resisted the establishment of an independent commission to investigate the Oct. 7 attacks. He has vowed to move ahead with overhauling Israel’s judicial system, a move that critics say could undermine the country’s liberal democracy. And his allies say they hope to permanently entrench Israeli rule in the West Bank and Gaza despite international condemnation.
The 77-year-old leader has dominated Israeli politics for decades. In recent days, he repeatedly suggested that the country could face annihilation without him in charge.
Here’s what else to watch:
Key issues: In a tumultuous campaign , several issues divided Israeli voters. Read more ›
West Bank and Gaza: As Israelis headed to the polls, Palestinians in the West Bank were under an Israeli military lockdown. Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza cannot vote in Israeli elections, but they may have much to lose if Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition stays in power. Read more ›
Poll times: Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party said it had asked the Central Election Committee to extend voting hours nationally beyond 10 p.m., an unheard-of move that election officials are unlikely to grant. Likud’s rivals argued that the highly unusual request was intended to sow doubt about the election’s integrity.
Election integrity: Mr. Netanyahu used racially charged language to cast suspicion over high turnout among Arab citizens and to encourage his base to go to the polls. Election officials said Tuesday that there had been no indication of widespread irregularities.
Trump weighs in: President Trump has endorsed Mr. Netanyahu , praising him as an important partner in the war against Iran and saying anyone else would be the “wrong leader” for Israel. Analysts were skeptical that the U.S. president’s intervention would sway many voters.
Turnout data may help explain why Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is worried about the pace of voting. With just over three hours until polls close, turnout in the five towns where his Likud party won its strongest support in 2022 was below the national rate by up to 10 percentage points.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel accused Arab citizens of “trying to steal the elections” on Tuesday, as he repeatedly used brazen and overtly racial appeals to push his right-wing base to vote.
“There are buses heading to the polls and long lines in Arab towns. Meanwhile, right-wing strongholds have yet to wake up!” he said on social media. “If we don’t go vote now, we will find ourselves with a government of Arab parties.”
Mr. Netanyahu has a long track record of appealing to his supporters by invoking the specter of the Arab vote. Arab citizens represent about 20 percent of Israel’s population, but have long complained that they are treated as second-class citizens and subject to discrimination.
In 2015, Mr. Netanyahu called on right-wing Israelis to vote because “Arabs were heading in droves to the polls.” His comments were widely condemned at home and abroad, including by the Obama administration. Mr. Netanyahu was accused of race-baiting and was forced to issue an apology for the remark.
On Tuesday, as initial data showed high turnout in Arab cities and towns, Mr. Netanyahu again used almost the same language to vilify Arab voters in several different statements over the course of the day.
“They say their voters are heading to the polls in droves. You too must head to the polls in droves,” Mr. Netanyahu said in a video statement, addressing right-wing voters.
Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List alliance of Arab parties, accused Mr. Netanyahu of “inciting against Arab citizens and undermining the legitimacy of our vote.”
“I’m telling you: the Arab community knows how to punish you,” Mr. Jabareen said. “Today we’re sending you and your bloodstained government packing.”
Arab citizens have tended to vote at lower rates than their Jewish counterparts. But in the run-up to this election, surveys suggested that they would turn out in higher numbers in an effort to vote out Mr. Netanyahu and his far-right allies. In Rahat, a large Bedouin town in southern Israel, turnout just before 5 p.m. was already at 60 percent — matching the town’s final turnout in the previous election.
Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party and some hard-right ministers in his government have also deployed incendiary messaging to appeal to supporters to vote.
The Likud party released images suggesting that there had been higher turnout in the Arab city of Rahat than Bat Yam, a Likud stronghold, which it called “a state of emergency.”
Another poster showed women in Muslim religious veils with the caption: “Right-wing voters, don’t stay home.”
Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, joined in the prime minister in trying to stoke fears over high Arab turnout. In a video filmed near the entrance of the Arab town of Kufr Qassim in central Israel, he said that Arab voters were heading to the polls “at hitherto never-before-seen rates,” threatening Israel’s Jewish character.
The prime minister also pointed to the arrests of three people suspected of planning to bribe voters for Raam, an Arab Israeli party, on Tuesday. Dean Livne, the acting director of Israel’s central elections committee, told reporters that there were no reports of widespread irregularities.
Lia Lapidot and Johnatan Reiss contributed reporting.
No party is expected to achieve a c

articles.title_orig: Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege
articles.title_zh: Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states on Monday sued Dollar General, accusing the budget retailer of charging customers more for products than it advertised.
The chain, which operates 21,000 stores nationwide, allegedly mislabeled prices for years, "extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges," the FTC alleged.
"Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement .
The FTC added that American consumers depend on Dollar General's advertised low prices to make ends meet on tight budgets, while prices that don't reflect advertised deals make it impossible for them to manage household finances.
The agency filed its complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, Dollar General's home state.
"Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store," Dollar General said in a statement. "As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement."
Dollar General said it was made aware of the FTC's investigation in early February.
According to the suit, thousands of Dollar General stores unlawfully overcharged shoppers.
Dollar General "has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve," the FTC and states allege in the suit. "Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country."
The company also faced thousands of consumer complaints claiming it failed to honor advertised prices at checkout, a sign Dollar General knowingly harmed customers, according to the FTC.
The suit seeks a permanent injunction, along with monetary and other relief.
In its statement, Dollar General said, "FTC staff also demanded a monetary amount that was untethered to — and orders of magnitude larger than — any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies."
The company said it "worked tirelessly and in good faith to resolve this matter without litigation," including an "alternative, and in our view, more reasonable, manner of calculating potential settlement ranges."
"Although we respect the FTC's role in protecting American consumers and the State representatives' role in protecting the citizens of their respective states, we will defend this litigation vigorously," it said.
The FTC leveled the unfair pricing allegations against Dollar General as other retailers face scrutiny over how they charge shoppers. Consumer advocates say retailers are developing new artificial intelligence-enabled technology that could be used to charge consumers different prices .
Groundwork Collaborative, a nonprofit think tank focused on economic policy, led an investigation into grocery-shopping platform Instacart and found that in a trial, it had used AI to simultaneously show customers different prices for the same goods from the same store.

articles.title_orig: Finland and Norway Hold ‘Frank’ Call With Putin on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Finland and Norway Hold ‘Frank’ Call With Putin on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Norway and Finland say they are not acting on behalf of other European leaders
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - a rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
The aim was looking at "future negotiations to help to end the war" in Ukraine, the offices of President Alexander Stubb and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said. Their initiative was not on behalf of "Europe as a whole".
After the call, Putin said "confrontational" EU and Nato policies were prolonging the war which began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken to the two Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin. Last week, Zelensky met them as well as US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
The Ukrainian leader said he was grateful for the "active support" of his Finnish and Norwegian counterparts.
Tuesday's 90-minute phone call was held from the Finnish capital Helsinki, and showed "big differences in views", StÃ¸re said.
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the call to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
The call was "frank and substantive", Stubb said, explaining that the war's outcome will "have a direct impact on our and the broader European security".
StÃ¸re added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
He - like Stubb and StÃ¸re - had agreed to continue their direct phone communication, the statement added.
Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
StÃ¸re said all their allies had been informed of the call ahead of time.
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "very sceptical" of Tuesday's dialogue, telling Danish broadcaster DR, it had not been "co-ordinated with any of the rest of us".
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates, was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US, Ukraine and its European allies have been souring since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia - allowing it to export oil to the US.
But last week, Stubb, StÃ¸re and Zelesnky met Witkoff in the Norwegian capital, before the US special envoy travelled on to St Petersburg to meet Putin.
Following the talks, Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to resume three-way negotiations that Russia had stopped for months.
After speaking to the two Nordic leaders, Zelensky said part of their discussions with Putin had centred on November's trilateral talks to be held in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky said he had discussed with them "various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security".
Stubb and StÃ¸re are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
As the US administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the European Union of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".

articles.title_orig: Who Is Zhang Yiming? China's Richest Person Again
articles.title_zh: Who Is Zhang Yiming? China's Richest Person Again
articles.content_orig:
Beijing — ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into artificial intelligence.
The rankings released by The Hurun Research Institute on Tuesday reflected that the country's high-tech sectors were rising while others, like the consumer sector and real estate, were under pressure.
The institute, which has published the list annually since 1999, found a record 1,529 people with more than 5 billion yuan (about $750 million), up 6.6% from last year.
The number of billionaires based on their net worth in U.S. dollars rose to 1,176, up 155 people - 176 more than in the U.S. That was slightly below the 1,185 people in 2021.
Zhang topped the list with $100 billion, up 43%, "almost all of it on the back of AI," and the amount was a record high for China's richest person, Rupert Hoogewerf, Hurun Report chairman, said in a statement. Hoogewerf noted that ByteDance's Doubao is China's most used AI assistant.
AI is the biggest single wealth engine on the list: 160 people - one in 10 - now make their money from AI, he said.
ByteDance is the parent company of popular short-video platforms TikTok and Douyin.
TikTok's U.S.-based operations were shifted to a new joint venture in January made up mostly of American investors due to years of national security-related concerns that almost got TikTok banned in the U.S. ByteDance still holds a minority stake in TikTok's U.S. arm.
One of the investors in TikTok's U.S. venture is Oracle, a tech company chaired by Larry Ellison. His son David Ellison is co-CEO of Skydance Corp., the parent company of CBS News.
Bottled water magnate Zhong Shanshan fell to second place on the list with $61 billion, down 23%, while Robin Zeng, chairman of CATL, the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, came in third, Hurun said.
Hurun cross-checked its information with entrepreneurs, regulators, industry experts and others to compile the list, while acknowledging limitations.
Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng, a new face on the list, ranked seventh. AI chipmaker Cambricon chair Chen Tianshi was 10th.
"This year's gains were polarised - entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink - a two-speed economy," Hoogewerf said.
China last week said its economy grew 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year ago, fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target for 2026. For the entire year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5%, down from last year's 5% expansion.
While some industries were thriving thanks to government support for technologies such as AI and electric vehicles, owners of small businesses reported tough times as their customers cut back on spending.
China's domestic demand has been weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market.
The Hurun list reflected that, as well.
Hoogewerf said Lei Jun, chairman of Chinese smart consumer electronics maker Xiaomi, was this year's "biggest faller," with his wealth halved to $25.1 billion. Consumer fortunes also fell across the board, Hoogewerf said.
"Today, for the first time ever, not a single mainland property developer remains in the Top 100 - the only property names left at the top are the Hong Kong landlord families," he said.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: 8-month Iran war looms over Israeli election as Egypt wades into Saudi's fight with the Houthis
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: 8-month Iran war looms over Israeli election as Egypt wades into Saudi's fight with the Houthis
articles.content_orig:
What to know about the Iran war:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, discussed working together on oil and gas projects as the two met in person at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum Summit in Moscow on Tuesday.
The two leaders "discussed expanding political, economic, trade and energy cooperation, including joint projects in the oil and gas sectors," according to a readout from the Iranian government .
Pezeshkian also discussed working together on natural gas exports. Iran ranks third in the world in natural gas production — 280 billion cubic meters per year, according to the president — behind only the U.S. and Russia.
"Pezeshkian emphasized that global developments necessitate joint technical-engineering cooperation and strategic governance across international energy markets," the government said, presumably referring to the war with the U.S.
Russia and Iran have worked together for years. As the war in Ukraine continues, Russia continues to purchase Shahed drones for use in attacks.
The two countries have rarely coordinated on energy projects, however, as both countries produce massive amounts of crude on their own. The timing of the discussion Tuesday in Russia is especially important though because Iran has been cut off from importing or exporting crude due to the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports.
France's deputy chief of mission in Tehran was this month subjected to "intimidation by individuals claiming to belong to the Iranian security forces," a diplomatic source told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.
The incident, the second involving French diplomats in Tehran in less than four months, highlights the sharp deterioration in relations between France and Iran.
In response to the mistreatment of the diplomat in early October, Iran's ambassador to France was summoned by the French foreign ministry, the source said, without specifying the exact date of the summons.
"He was reminded in the strongest terms that we expect the Iranian authorities to take all necessary measures to guarantee the security of our personnel and premises," the source said.
French magazine Le Point , which first reported the incident, said the diplomat was forcibly stopped in the street by members of Iran's security forces, in breach of his diplomatic status. The encounter culminated in what the magazine described as a forceful interrogation.
The episode follows a July incident involving two French diplomats based in Tehran.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot accused the Iranian authorities at the time of having "detained them without reason for several hours," adding one of them had been "physically manhandled."
Iran said at the time the diplomats had been "briefly questioned" by security services after attending a "meeting with several individuals wanted by the authorities," and denounced French "interference … under the pretext of engaging with civil society."
The Iran-backed Houthis claimed Thursday that they struck three different airports in southwestern Saudi Arabia, and repelled an advance by Saudi-affiliated forces from the southern direction of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on X that the group's forces had "succeeded in targeting two military transport aircraft with two ballistic missiles: the first at Najran Airport and the second at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait," both of which are in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives, by the grace of God," he added.
In a separate statement on X , Saree said Houthi forces earlier thwarted an attempted advance by what he described as Saudi enemy forces "from the southern direction of Bab al-Mandab," the gateway to the Red Sea.
"These force concentrations were targeted with a number of ballistic missiles and heavy weapons, resulting in large numbers of dead and wounded," he said.
In a third statement Tuesday, Saree claimed the Houthis had struck Abha International Airport, also in the Saudi southwest.
"The strike was accurate and led to the disruption of air traffic at the airport," he said.
An oil tanker has caught fire after being caught in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's navy said on Tuesday.
"Hours ago, a rogue oil tanker that had switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited and unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz struck naval mines, sustaining damage and catching fire," the navy's public relations office said.
"The Strait of Hormuz is unsafe and closed to rogue ships and vessels attempting to pass through without coordination," it added.
Iran has repeatedly said it will only allow vessels to pass through the waterway if they coordinate with authorities. The U.S. has urged shippers to use a southern route through the strait that Tehran regards as illegal.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is in "perfect health," describing him as energetic, hopeful and composed following a meeting.
Khamenei was seriously wounded in the strikes that killed his father, Ali Khamenei, sources told CBS News in March. He has not been seen in public since the start of the war.
"The leader is in perfect health, and truly, what I observed during the meeting was a strong, energetic, hopeful and resolute spirit, along with inner peace," Ghalibaf said Tuesday.
"These qualities were fully evident in the leader," he added, "and I felt with all my being that this resolve and inner peace reflect a strong faith in Almighty God and a deep belief in the people."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Tuesday they had downed two ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh, the Saudi capital.
"Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi group toward the capital, Riyadh," spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki wrote in a post on X .
Multiple explosions were heard in Riyadh on Tuesday, journalists from the AFP news agency said.
Residents received a text-message alert on their mobile phones warning of an "aerial threat" and instructing them to seek shelter.
This latest attack follows weeks of strikes by the Houthis, who claimed Tuesday to have struck a refinery in eastern Saudi Arabia.
A Kuwaiti State Security and Terrorism Criminal Court sentenced three men to death on Monday over an alleged plot to assassinate First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad Al-Yousef, with prosecutors accusing the defendants of spying for Iran, communicating with Iranian-linked entities and joining Hezbollah, two judicial sources told the AFP news agency Tuesday.
The court also sentenced eight other defendants to varying prison terms.
Those sentenced to death included cleric and National Islamic Alliance Secretary-General Hussein Abdullah Al-Maatouq and two other men. One of the defendants had previously been convicted of terrorism in 2016 and later received a pardon before being arrested again in April, the sources said.
According to Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Rai , the defendants were accused of communicating with Iran and entities allegedly operating in its interests, including Lebanese group Hezbollah, to carry out hostile acts against Kuwait following the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on Feb. 28, at the beginning of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
The defendants were also accused of joining Hezbollah, a banned group in Kuwait, while knowing its objectives, and of engaging in activities allegedly intended to undermine the country's political, social and economic order and harm its national interests.
Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Qabas reported prosecutors accused the defendants of attempting to use explosives to carry out the alleged assassination plot and spread panic. One defendant was separately accused of attempting to bring explosives into the country to enable the others to carry out the alleged operation.

articles.title_orig: From 'Mobut' to Mao, Mbappe dictator meme turns self-mockery into China storm
articles.title_zh: From 'Mobut' to Mao, Mbappe dictator meme turns self-mockery into China storm
articles.content_orig:
By WILL HALLOWELL, NEWS REPORTER
Published: 04:53 EDT, 27 October 2026 | Updated: 11:40 EDT, 27 October 2026
Kylian Mbappe has been dropped by Chinese brands while state TV stations have suspended all LaLiga broadcasts following a joke about Mao Zedong.
A video circulated online in which the French Real Madrid superstar apparently mocked the former Chinese Communist Party leader.
In the footage, he said the funniest internet meme he had seen was of his face photo-shopped onto that of 'some guy – I think he's a Chinese dictator'.
Mbappe has apologised for the 'ill-judged' joke, saying he has 'deep respect' for China and its history.
Meanwhile LaLiga president Javier Medrano has also been forced to weigh in and apologise to China, describing Mbappe's comments as 'offensive' and adding that the Spanish league is 'taking measures... to overcome this situation'.
In China, jokes about Mao – the country's founding leader who died in 1976 – are considered disrespectful and remain a social taboo.
Mbappe had brand deals with the drinks giant Dongpeng and China's largest dairy producer Mengniu, who have now cut ties with the 27-year-old.
Adverts showing AI-generated images of the France captain drinking a Dongpeng sports drink were regularly shown in China during this year's World Cup.
Chinese brands have dropped French football star Kylian Mbappe after he 'joked' about former leader Mao Zedong
In China, jokes about Mao – the country's founding leader who died in 1976 – are considered disrespectful and remain a social taboo
The meme that football fans had created photoshopping Mbappe's face onto Mao, which he references in the video
Those firms have now dropped Mbappe after accusing him of offending the nation.
China Media Group, the state broadcaster, has also reportedly stopped broadcasting LaLiga matches and advertisements involving Mbappe, citing the Frenchman's 'seriously negative conduct' concerning China, according to EFE .
Dongpeng said in a statement: 'Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments.'
The drinks giant added that 'with immediate effect we are terminating all co-operation with Kylian Mbappe'.
Mengniu said in a statement: 'With immediate effect our company is terminating all co-operation with Kylian Mbappe.
'Mengniu firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.'
Until this incident, Mbappe was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of followers on social media.
Mbappe is fondly nicknamed 'Guigui', the Chinese translation of 'Turtle', due to his perceived similarity to one of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.
A bus featuring Mbappe for Dongpeng's Bushuila electrolyte drink is seen on a street in Shanghai
Mengniu milk products are seen on a shelf at a store in Beijing. The brand has dropped Mbappe after his 'joke' about Mao
Mbappe seen on bottles of one of Dongpeng's electrolyte drinks
The centre-forward's comments in the video were an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappe superimposed on an image of Mao, one of several using the footballer's face and other historical figures.
In a statement on Tuesday, Mbappe said: 'During a recent interview, I reacted to an image of myself.
'My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.
'I apologise to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention.
'I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history. I am sincerely sorry.'
LaLiga president Mr Medrano said: 'From LaLiga, we deeply regret the statements made by Kylian Mbappe that have caused discomfort and offense in China.
'We understand the harm caused and, on behalf of LaLiga I wish to convey our sincere apologies to the Chinese people.
'For many years, we have built a relationship of respect, trust and co-operation with China, its authorities, its sports institutions, its audiovisual operators, and millions of fans of Spanish football.
'We cannot allow an individual action to tarnish that relationship or harm the more than 20 clubs in our professional competitions and millions of Chinese fans.
'We are taking the measures within our reach and working directly with our partners and interlocutors in China to overcome this situation.
'Our commitment to China, its people, and its institutions is steadfast. A relationship built over so many years cannot be damaged by a single episode.'
Four topics related to Mbappe were still among the top ten trending searches on China's social media platform Weibo on Tuesday morning.
Some users called for China to 'blacklist' Mbappe and reduce his commercial value to zero. These comments received hundreds of likes.
Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappe's face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to call the shots at the teams he plays for.
In an interview with L'Equipe last month, Mbappe said that while some aspects of the meme trend were harmless fun, the viral ones depicting him as a dictator showed 'a lack of political and human awareness'.
When asked about the incident, a spokesman for China's Foreign Ministry said that words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people 'will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society'.
Mbappe has now apologised for the offence caused by his joke, which the France star admitted was 'ill-judged'
'Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappe' has been the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo.
One Weibo user said that the 'extremely serious wrong remarks... crossed the red line. They are completely unacceptable'.
Others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappe's image from their energy drink bottles.
Dongqiudi, one of China's biggest online football outlets, said on Monday evening that Mbappe's remarks were 'offensive to China and the Chinese people' and 'have hurt the feelings of Chinese football fans and the Chinese people'.
Mbappe in September addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator, in an interview with French sports newspaper L'Equipe.
He said: 'There's a part of it that's funny. You can tell that, for some people, it's all in good fun.
'But there is another part that's a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history.'
The 27-year-old added: 'Being compared to individuals who murder others, or who have brought misery to millions upon millions of people – well, I don't think I've ever done anything like that in my life.'
The furore in China came a day after Mbappe lost out to Harry Kane for the Ballon d'Or, the most prestigious individual award in football.
Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there.
Former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island's vice president and current president Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media.
Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.
Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.
Chinese media outlets reacted with fury to Mbappe's comments on Tuesday.
'A remark about an internet meme has triggered a backlash among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence,' state media outlet China Daily said.
'What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it,' the state-backed Global Times said.

articles.title_orig: Boeing Stock Plunges After Earnings. 737 Progress Is Not Fast Enough.
articles.title_zh: Boeing Stock Plunges After Earnings. 737 Progress Is Not Fast Enough.
articles.content_orig:
Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.
CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected becuase of the wings production pace.
Boeing stock was down about 9% during the call.
"I know everybody wants us to go faster but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.
Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

articles.title_orig: Iran talks Middle East security, urges region to get US influence out
articles.title_zh: Iran talks Middle East security, urges region to get US influence out
articles.content_orig:
The State Department has ordered non-emergency government personnel and their families to evacuate Saudi Arabia following a surge in missile and drone strikes targeting civilian airports and critical infrastructure across the kingdom.
In a security alert issued Tuesday, the U.S. warned that ongoing hostilities by Iran-backed Houthi forces have caused severe travel disruptions and civilian casualties, prompting strict travel restrictions for American personnel and warnings of wider regional spillover.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," according to the alert.
"The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."
Flight operations remain severely disrupted across major transit hubs, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport , where only limited routes are running, alongside significant delays at facilities in Jeddah and Dammam.
U.S. officials urged private citizens to exercise extreme caution, consider overland transit alternatives via operational borders like the King Fahd Causeway, and strictly abide by local regulations barring the filming or sharing of attack sites and counter-missile activity.
Vice President JD Vance defended President Donald Trump's bold midterm election year pressure on Iran's threats in the Strait of Hormuz, acknowledging its causing higher gas prices globally, but warning the U.S. cannot be held hostage every time a Middle East leader "throws a tantrum."
"I want to speak to the voters who are undecided: You'll hear many say that gas prices are too high," Vance told his rally in Howell, Michigan , on Tuesday. "Ladies and gentlemen, I understand that it's true, but the deeper truth is that the price of gas goes up each time a foreign leader in the Middle East throws a tantrum.
"That's been true, by the way, since before I was alive, starting in the 1970s.
"But what's different? What's different about this country's and this leaderships' agenda ?
"And what's different about the Democrats is that the Democrats talk about high gas prices, even though their policies have made us more vulnerable to the foreign despots in the first place."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is traveling Tuesday aboard Air Force One with President Donald Trump in his concurrent capacity as national security adviser, securing direct access to the commander-in-chief, an administration official confirmed to Fox News.
With Trump maintaining an active domestic travel schedule ahead of the midterms, the transit time provides a dedicated window for high-level national security consultations.
"He needs time with the president on all kinds of issues," according to a White House official.
"The president will be on the go, so being on the plane with him gives him a chance to talk to him about these items."
The in-flight briefings come at a critical juncture for U.S. Middle East strategy.
Over the last 24 hours alone, the White House has confronted an escalating maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz marked by active Iranian mine detonations, Houthi strikes targeting Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery, and the emergency evacuation of non-essential U.S. personnel from the kingdom.
Fox News' Gillian Turner contributed to this report.
President Donald Trump highlighted incoming shipments of Venezuelan crude Tuesday as a direct economic cushion against rising fuel prices spurred by the 9-month-old conflict with Iran, pointing to alternative energy imports during a campaign departure for Texas.
Speaking to reporters ahead of rallies alongside Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Trump praised recent surges in consumer confidence before confirming plans to showcase an arriving oil tanker carrying Venezuelan crude destined for processing at Gulf Coast facilities.
"We took over Venezuela very successfully, and they've sent me as a gift, a boatload of a million barrels of oil, and I'm giving that to the United States of America," Trump told reporters on the tarmac from Joint Base Andrews, framing the imports as a tangible benefit of his administration's pressure campaign.
"We're going to accept a million barrels of oil , and I'm going to give it to you people to use it the way you want. And we're going to have oil prices are going to be dropping very sharply."
The administration has increasingly relied on Western Hemisphere energy flows to offset global supply contractions caused by maritime blockades in the Strait of Hormuz and repeated strikes by Iran-aligned proxies on regional Gulf infrastructure.
With domestic pump prices edging above previous-term averages just a week before the November midterms, the White House has maintained that foreign oil seizures, increased Caribbean imports, and record domestic production will neutralize temporary spikes until the Middle East war is resolved.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is warning about voter turnout in the elections underway Tuesday.
"We're at war for our home 🚨," Netanyahu added in a second post. "Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections.
"Go out and vote, recover it!!"
Cars flying Netanyahu's Likud party flags drove through Jerusalem blaring the Islamic call to prayer and urging supporters to cast their ballots because "Arabs are voting," witnesses said.
"If we don't wake up now, we'll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi," Netanyahu wrote in a post, referring to two leading Palestinian Arab politicians in Israel.
Turnout reached 55.7% in the first nine hours of voting, the elections committee said, the fastest pace on record.
Arabs, mostly of Palestinian heritage, make up about 21% of Israel's population of 10 million and have traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis.
Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said strong turnout among Israel's Arab minority would "pave the way for an alternative government and change the grave reality."
Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Arab Balad party, wrote on X that long lines outside polling stations should bring "pride and joy to anyone who believed in democracy."
"We are receiving all these inciting messages from the petty racists, Ben-Gvir, Netanyahu, and their partners," he added. " What are they afraid of ? This is actually an excellent sight, it is good for democracy."
In a statement, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir described the level of Arab voter turnout as "crazy," urging supporters to vote for his Jewish Power party if they wanted the country to be Jewish and Zionist .
Smotrich's Religious Zionism party said the finance minister had suspended his election day campaigning to convene an emergency meeting to discuss what it described as unusually high turnout among Arab voters.
Reuters contributed to this report.
House Budget Committee Chairman Jodey Arrington , R-Texas, strongly defended President Donald Trump's military confrontation with Tehran on Tuesday.
Arrington argued that decades of bipartisan caution had allowed Iran’s regional aggression to metastasize unchecked, insisting that Trump prioritized long-term American safety over near-term political risks.
"Look, we had a precipitous decline in the cost of energy leading up to the Iranian conflict," Arrington told FOX Business ' "Big Money in the Morning" on Tuesday.
"I think the American people understand that for almost 50 years, we gave that terrorist regime a pass. I think this president recognized that he was going to be the last commander in chief to address this situation before we had a Kim Jong Un in the Middle East, essentially.
"And so he was willing to take the risk, quite frankly. Thank God we have a commander in chief that's willing to do things that aren't in his political interest on account of the security interest of the American people."

articles.title_orig: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say
articles.title_zh: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say
articles.content_orig:
Far-right senator on plane to US after missing deadline to hand over his passport since loss to Lula
The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
A report by the news website Metrópoles , citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.
Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.
Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that he was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.
“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.
The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.
Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday.
A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.
A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.
The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”
One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.
The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.
As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.
The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.
Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.
The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.
Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.
after newsletter promotion
Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.
“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.
Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.
“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.
Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.
Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.
Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.
Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.
Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.
“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.

articles.title_orig: Two Nordic leaders urge Putin to end Ukraine war in rare direct contact by Europeans
articles.title_zh: Two Nordic leaders urge Putin to end Ukraine war in rare direct contact by Europeans
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
President Vladimir Putin received a joint call from the leaders of Norway and Finland on Tuesday as they urged him to end the war in Ukraine, sparking rare contact between Europe and Russia.
The aim of the call, initiated by the offices of President Alexander Stubb and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, was to look at “future negotiations to help end the war”.
Store said he and Stubb “stressed the importance of de-escalation” as both leaders voiced strong support for Ukraine, speaking to President Volodymyr Zelensky straight after Putin.
Tuesday’s “frank and substantive” 90 minute phone call was conducted from Helsinki, Finland’s capital, and showed “big differences in views”, according to Store
Following the call, Putin said the duration of the conflict , which has been raging on for four years, has been prolonged by “confrontational” EU and NATO policies, and that a “just and lasting peace” would only be possible if Russia’s interests were considered.
Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on how to end the war that began with Russia's invasion in February 2022, and long-range airstrikes by both sides have increased this year while battle lines have remained largely static.
"The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact ⁠on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.
The Kremlin's readout of the call did not suggest any softening of Putin's position.
"It was emphasised that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account," it said.
"At the same time, ⁠attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities."
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Tuesday's call had offered nothing new on the `Ukraine conflict, which he said was likely to escalate, and that European countries were simply seeking a role in the negotiation process.
Western European leaders have mostly refused to talk to Putin, hoping to isolate him. But they have been sidelined in peace efforts led by US President Donald Trump, who is seen in many European capitals as unpredictable and prone to side with Putin at Ukraine's expense.
That perception has been reinforced by deals this month in which Putin agreed to supply Russian diesel to the United States and Trump eased sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine has also complained of disruption to intelligence-sharing by the US and to satellite internet services on which its military relies.
Gerhard Mangott, an Austrian political analyst, said European governments had "manoeuvred themselves into a dead end" when it came to finding a solution to the war, and Tuesday's call was an effort to establish a channel for dialogue.
He drew attention to remarks by Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov on Sunday suggesting Europe should be part of discussions. "I interpret this as a shift in Russia's position, given that Moscow had previously consistently rejected the ⁠idea of discussing a settlement of the war in Ukraine with the Europeans," Mangott said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been coordinated with Kyiv and was "the right approach".
"We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process," he said, adding that he also hoped a local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky could "pave the way to other steps in the peace process."
But Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she saw no signs that Russia wanted peace, adding: "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo."
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said other European leaders were not informed of the talks . "My impression is that everyone wants peace, except for Putin himself. I have quite low expectations for this type of conversation," Kristersson told Swedish daily DN.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had told Stubb and Stoere that "absolute caution and vigilance are necessary in such contacts".
Stubb and Stoere said they acted as leaders of their respective countries and not on ‌behalf of Europe, and had "consulted thoroughly with all our partners."
Russia has frequently accused European governments of stoking the war by arming Ukraine and refusing direct talks. A source close to the Kremlin said French President Emmanuel Macron had been the last EU leader to speak with Putin — in a summer call that yielded no results and was not ‌made public.
The source said Putin told Stubb and Stoere that the European involvement was `welcome and that the war needed to end "taking into account the realities on the ground".
Asked what this meant, the person said it signified that Russia would not compromise ⁠over its aim to capture the whole of Ukraine's Donbas region. The Europeans responded by saying a "just" peace was needed, the source said.
The two Nordic leaders may be less encumbered than their peers from larger European states such as Britain, France and Germany, whose ties with Moscow have deteriorated further.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said attempts to end the war "can never find solutions without Ukraine", and must include European countries.
Merz said Germany and other European states wanted to establish a format to speak to Russia's government and that Norway and Finland were playing "a very constructive role" in that effort. The Kremlin said Putin, Stoere and Stubb would keep in touch by phone.

articles.title_orig: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.title_zh: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.content_orig:
US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title_orig: India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
articles.title_zh: India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
articles.content_orig:
New Delhi, India – India’s armed forces are locked in multiple ongoing face-offs with the Chinese army along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the chief of India’s paramilitary border force guarding the Himalayan frontier with China has said.
The remarks late last week by Shatrujeet Kapur, the director-general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) paramilitary force, come nearly four months after local civil society groups in the remote northeastern region told Al Jazeera that Chinese forces were increasingly encroaching on Indian territory and denying Indian troops access to patrolling points, angering locals.
Chinese President Xi Jinping was in New Delhi last month – his first trip to India in seven years – for the BRICS summit, where he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines, as the two capitals pursued a cautious thaw in bilateral ties. That thaw is partly driven by United States President Donald Trump’s trade war, which has pushed nuclear-armed rivals Beijing and New Delhi closer.
Yet the alleged Chinese incursions into India underscore how, despite warm handshakes in New Delhi, tensions along the 3,500-kilometre (2,200-mile) border between the neighbours threaten to undercut efforts to normalise ties.
They also pose a major political challenge to Modi, who has built an image as being strong on national security, but who has in recent years faced difficult questions about the relationship with China.
The face-offs with Chinese forces in Arunachal Pradesh – that “still continue”, according to Kapur – come six years after at least 20 Indian troops were killed in hand-to-hand combat with Chinese forces in mountainous Ladakh.
Though satellite imagery and multiple accounts, including from within the Indian security establishment, have since pointed to China effectively taking control of parts of previously disputed territory since that fight, the Modi government has refused to concede that it has given up any land.
And five days after Kapur’s comments on recent standoffs, the Indian government is yet to confirm the nature of the border tensions, instead offering more boilerplate criticisms of China.
Kapur, the ITBP chief, was speaking at a felicitation ceremony for the paramilitary force’s personnel, where he revealed that commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the border with China.
Arunachal Pradesh’s remote Upper Subansiri region – where the ongoing face-offs are reported – had seen the first clash between independent India and China in August 1959, which killed at least two Indian soldiers.
Then-Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke of the remoteness of the region in his account of the clash, when he told Parliament that the border post under Chinese attack was roughly three weeks’ march from the nearest roadhead.
The decades-long India-China border dispute is rooted in a British-drawn border, called the McMahon Line. In 1914, British India and Tibet, not under Chinese control at the time, signed the Simla Convention, demarcating their border. Since gaining independence in 1947, India has treated the McMahon Line as its border with China. But China, which came under communist rule in 1949, rejects the line as the boundary with India, arguing that Tibet lacked the authority to conclude the agreement independently.
Beijing claims the entire state of Arunachal Pradesh and refers to it as “South Tibet” or “Zangnan”. China also controls Aksai Chin, a slice of the disputed Kashmir region that India and Pakistan claim in full.
With their territorial claims unresolved, India and China signed an agreement in 1993 to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), their de facto boundary from 1962, pending a final border settlement. They continue to disagree over its precise alignment.
Those differences were never bridged in the following years, keeping the disputed frontier a persistent flashpoint in relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.
The dispute erupted again into a deadly confrontation in June 2020, when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in eastern Ladakh, with both sides accusing the other of crossing the LAC. At least 20 Indian soldiers were killed, and China later acknowledged four deaths among its troops.
Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, said that border tensions amid a thaw in bilateral relations now appear as “part of a pattern” – “likely a pressure tactic by Beijing,” he added.
And due to the undemarcated border, “stand-offs are bound to occur from time to time, some of which may go out of hand”, Donthi warned.
But the 2020 clash also pushed Modi into a corner domestically, as the opposition parties pressured the government over its opaque handling of China. The Modi government also faced opposition complaints over restrictions on parliamentary scrutiny, questions about whether intelligence agencies had detected the Chinese troop build-up, and limited disclosure of operational details.
Contradictions between the government’s own stand and Modi’s claims also prompted accusations that he was trying to minimise – or even hide – the scale of the crisis along the border.
On June 17, 2020, soon after the Galwan clash, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar spoke to his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.
“The Chinese side sought to erect a structure in Galwan Valley on our side of the LAC,” the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said after the phone call. “While this became a source of dispute, the Chinese side took premeditated and planned action that was directly responsible for the resulting violence and casualties. It reflected an intent to change the facts on ground in violation of all our agreements to not change the status quo.”
Yet two days later, Modi said on Twitter, now X, that “neither has anyone been able to enter our territory, nor is anyone still on our territory” – an assertion that disputed the foreign ministry’s account. If no Chinese troops had crossed the LAC, why had Indian soldiers been forced to fight them, the opposition and other strategic analysts asked?
The government has never answered those questions, with Modi’s office only issuing a clarification that the prime minister meant that there were no Chinese troops still in Indian territory after the clash.
Six years since the Ladakh clash, the Chinese incursion has returned to challenge Modi’s strongman image at home – which has already taken a hit from youth-led protests in the country that forced out Modi’s education minister in July this year.
In his address, ITBP chief Kapur also recalled the 2020 clash, outlining a specialised training programme “to better equip personnel to deal with” a Ladakh-like situation.
Kapur, who is due to retire this week, also warned that China’s frontier military capabilities had advanced – and Indian forces may not be able to take a fight head-on by traditional methods.
The Crisis Group’s Donthi said that the Modi government “presents an image of a hard security state with zero tolerance for national security failures”. but “the power differential with China is quite sharp, so it tends to downplay any event that reflects poorly”.
The opposition Congress party’s top leader in Arunachal Pradesh state, Bosiram Siram, said that Chinese troops have intruded nearly 50km (31 miles) deep into Indian territory in remote Upper Subansiri.
A Siram-led party delegation visited border areas in August after initial reports of China’s incursions, and Siram added that “Chinese personnel are stationed up there”, referring to Indian territory.
“You can see the [Chinese] Army. They are on top of the mountains, while we are down below,” Siram added.
In response to the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that “the situation in India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns”. He did not comment on

articles.title_orig: DeepMind unveils Genie 4 world model promising more realistic physics and humans
articles.title_zh: DeepMind unveils Genie 4 world model promising more realistic physics and humans
articles.content_orig:
Last year, Google DeepMind sent gaming stocks tumbling with the reveal of its Genie 3 world model . Since then, world models have become a major focus of AI labs around the world, but Google isn’t resting on its laurels. Researchers have been hard at work on an updated model that improves on Genie 3 in almost every way. And if you pay Google enough money, you might actually get to use Genie 4 before too long.
It’s easy to look at the output of Genie 4 and see a video game, which is why Genie 3 caused so much consternation in the gaming industry. DeepMind doesn’t think about it that way, though. According to Google , world models are a key element in the march toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). A world model creates a virtual world, but it doesn’t require pre-rendering environments or programming interactive elements. You simply tell the model what you want, and it generates the experience frame by frame in real time as you explore it.
DeepMind says this technology could create infinite training environments for physical robots or unlock new avenues of rapid prototyping for creative fields. Of course, that requires the model to accurately simulate what you want. Genie 4 has several improvements that make its simulations more useful, and that’s thanks in part to Google’s updated Gemini models.
When you prompt a world into existence in Genie 4, it leverages Gemini 3.8 Flash as a guiding agent to break down goals and evaluate each output frame. This helps keep the simulation on track, letting you move through varying environments without losing the original context. However, DeepMind notes that Genie 4 worlds still only remain consistent for a couple of minutes before they forget how things started.
Like Genie 3, the new version supports changing the parameters midstream. You can change the weather, add elements, or move the camera, and Gemini will help steer the simulation with each update. This is similar to the way reasoning models generate additional internal prompts to zero in on the right output tokens.
The physics in AI-generated video can sometimes look a bit unnatural, but DeepMind says Genie 4 has reached a new level of realism. Genie 4 can apparently do a better job with elements like aerodynamics and collisions, which makes the simulations more useful and visually appealing. People appearing in these simulations should also look less uncanny, with more natural movement and responses to the changing environment.
Genie 4 is also the first DeepMind world model with native audio. Videos will have ambient background sounds, and you can specify audio elements in your prompt. The biggest leap, if it works, is the addition of human speech. DeepMind promises that Genie 4 will be able to create interactive dialog that adapts as you change the simulation. Realistic speech in standard AI video was a major shift in realism, and now a similar revolution may be coming to Google’s world models.
DeepMind is careful to point out that world models are still an active area of research—Genie 3 never expanded beyond the very limited Project Genie web experience. However, the team has been working with a small group of trusted testers to build toward a wider release for Genie 4. Access will start expanding soon, but there’s no specific timeline yet. It won’t be cheap, though.
Google plans to roll out Genie 4 for developers via the Gemini API and AI Studio, but pricing isn’t yet available. Consumers will be able to get access, but it will roll out in phases with Google’s most expensive AI Ultra plans, which start at $100 per month. Google may expand access to AI Pro and AI Plus plans eventually. This will still be handled through Project Genie, which will limit how much you can do with Genie. There’s a waitlist for users who are interested in getting early access.

articles.title_orig: More than 120 years ago today, NYC opened its first underground train
articles.title_zh: More than 120 years ago today, NYC opened its first underground train
articles.content_orig:
One of the world’s oldest public transit systems, one of the world’s longest subway systems, and, of course, one of the world’s most-used metro systems: the New York City Subway.
On October 27, 1904, New York City Mayor George McClellan inaugurated the city’s new and innovative rapid transit system. Boston was the first to build a subway in the United States in 1897, but when the New York City subway opened, it became the largest in America.
The Interborough Rapid Transit Company (IRT) won a fifty-year operating lease and began construction on the NY underground transit system in 1900.
The construction work took four years, and the initial line ran through Manhattan from City Hall to West 145th Street. Local newspapers called it “the finest subway in the world,” praising its artistic and architectural features. And while some newspapers celebrated it, many others raised health concerns, focusing on poor air ventilation and the potential spread of infectious diseases like tuberculosis.
On its opening day, by 7 p.m., the subway was open to the public, and more than 100,000 people paid a nickel each for their first ride.
From 1904 to 1925 , private corporations ran the Subway. The IRT extended it into the Bronx and Brooklyn, and the Brooklyn Rapid Transit Company (BRT) shifted from railroad lines to subway lines in Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens.
In 1913, the IRT and BRT signed dual contracts with the city to improve existing lines, but after a while, BRT went bankrupt, and many of its subway lines were taken over by the Brooklyn-Manhattan Transit Corporation BMT.
The New York City Transit Authority (NYCTA) took ownership in 1953. And about ten years later, the state-level Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) took control of the NYCTA. Since then, the subway has been controlled by the MTA.
The system now has 36 lines and 472 stations in operation.
