articles.title_orig: Protesters enter Serbian pro-Vucic TV station, call for arrest of editor
articles.title_zh: Protesters enter Serbian pro-Vucic TV station, call for arrest of editor
articles.content_orig:
Pro-Vucic tabloid Informer pushed the state’s line for years. This week, the audience pushed back.
On October 26, less than 24 hours after Serbian strongman Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in the snap parliamentary elections against the student-led Students’ List, dozens of protesters stormed the offices of Informer , a pro-government tabloid and TV network.
Among them was the mother of one of the 16 victims of the Novi Sad railway station disaster, according to AFP . For context, the deadly collapse of the railway station roof in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city, in November 2024, was widely blamed on corruption. It triggered Serbia’s largest student-led protests since the fall of Slobodan Milosevic in 2000, which eventually snowballed into the political movement that ousted Vucic.
Protesters interrupted Informer ’s regular broadcast, and in a video circulating on social media , one man demanded that editor-in-chief Dragan Vucicevic “apologise sincerely to his free Serbian people.” After brief clashes with police, the crowd dispersed.
For months, pro-government outlets like Informer cast protesting students as dangerous actors conspiring to destabilise Serbia. On Sunday, those students won.
According to the BBC , with 97 percent of polling stations counted, “students had won 2.25 million votes (53 percent) and the former ruling party 1.67 million (39 percent)”, on a near-record turnout of almost 70 percent, quoting Serbia's election commission. Vucic, who had resigned the presidency to run for prime minister, conceded less than two hours after polls closed.
This is not the first time protesters have gone after Informer. In March 2025, students gathered outside its headquarters for a rally. One speaker at the rally, as reported by N1 TV , said Informer is “a political newsletter disguised as a media outlet.” Her sharper point was that hatred is its main rhetoric, creating an atmosphere in which violence becomes legitimate. “They don’t inform, they persecute,” she said. Students read out provisions of the Code of Journalists of Serbia and hung parts of it on the gate.
The protester wasn’t wrong. In a June 2026 Reuters Institute report , Snjezana Milivojevic, a retired professor of public opinion and media studies at the University of Belgrade, writes that pro-government tabloids have often been used to “discredit dissenting voices, run smear campaigns” and amplify nationalist and anti-EU narratives.
Informer , she notes, was among three tabloids the Press Council named for infringing the Code of Ethics in the second half of 2025, with 1,456 violations in its case. Since launching a cable news channel in November 2024, it has reached 14 percent of the report’s survey respondents weekly offline and 12 percent online, with the lowest public trust of any brand surveyed at 19 percent. Reach without credibility is seemingly the business model.
How the press was captured
Milivojevic writes that Serbia’s media landscape has “deteriorated significantly during the ongoing political crisis.” Reporters Without Borders tells the same story, ranking Serbia 104th of 180 countries in 2026, down from 96th in 2025, with the political indicator sliding from 141st to 151st. In its survey, RSF had called Vucic a “press freedom predator.”
The government, Milivojevic writes, responded to the protests by “tightening control over the judiciary, media, and universities,” with “over 1,636 arrests reported between June and September 2025.” The media ownership structure tells the rest of the story.
According to Milivojevic’s report, all national commercial channels are owned by companies tied to the political elites, which “effectively closes the mainstream media to reporting critical of the government.”  State-owned Telekom Srbija has bought more than 30 TV channels in a year and became, in her words, “the major delivery platform, and one of the top advertisers in the country.”
The two critical channels, N1 and TV Nova , are owned by United Group, “an international telecom and media company”, according to the report. Vucic regularly targeted them “as anti-Serbian or even terrorist media,” notes Milivojevic. A leaked conversation from August 2025 caught United Group’s new CEO agreeing to dismiss its media head at Vucic’s request. On April 6, 2026, N1’s director of news, Igor Bozic, was replaced, and journalists’ unions and media watchers said steps like these could lead to the “neutering or shutting down of N1.”
What we have here is concentration of ownership, state money as leverage, owners who flinch, and a prime-time chorus that brands dissenters as enemies of the nation. If you’re a consumer of mainstream TV media in India, this all seems rather too familiar.
Furthermore, RSF counted at least 100 physical attacks on reporters covering the 2025 protests, many by police officers, and noted illegal phone hacking of journalists by the intelligence service and police.
None of this makes Monday’s scenes simple. A crowd entering a newsroom, even that of a propaganda outlet, is a troubling image, and press freedom groups will rightly say so. But the anger at Informer ’s door was built by an outlet that treated fellow citizens as targets.

articles.title_orig: Apple Creator Studio gets powerful new AI features using OpenAI models
articles.title_zh: Apple Creator Studio gets powerful new AI features using OpenAI models
articles.content_orig:
Apple Creator Studio updates have today been announced, with what the company describes as “powerful new AI features” using a combination of Apple Intelligence and OpenAI models.
Final Cut Pro for Mac will also include built-in MotionVFX to provide a large collection of visual effects, transitions, and motion graphics tools …
Apple announced the updates alongside the new iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro powered by the M6 chip. It will be a free update for existing subscribers at some point in November.
Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro.
Music creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library.
Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language.
Keynote, Pages, and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants 2 that understand document context and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for workflow automation. They also add stock video in the Content Hub and new premium themes and templates.
The headline news here is MotionVFX for Final Cut Pro.
Final Cut Pro for Mac now integrates MotionVFX directly into the app, giving editors access to thousands of elements, including templates with unique themes, stylish graphics, titles, and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading. Editors can also tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock videos, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow.
Also notable is that the inclusion of OpenAI models alongside Apple Intelligence.
A new intelligent assistant powered by a combination of Apple-built models and OpenAI joins Logic Pro for Mac, helping creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.
Visual productivity apps receive a new generation of intelligence features for subscribers, including an intelligent assistant, built on Apple models and OpenAI, directly within Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant understands document context to help users accomplish more without leaving their work.
In Keynote, the intelligent assistant helps with designing, animating, and refining slides. In Pages, it drafts, restructures, and fine-tunes written content. In Numbers, it calculates, visualizes, and organizes data; recommends suitable chart types with a one-tap preview; and builds custom tables using world knowledge.
New MCP support, built on this platform, enables external AI agents and tools to read content, perform edits, and execute automated actions directly in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers.
Apple hasn’t announced an exact launch date for the new features, instead saying that it will be “this November.”

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Issues Emergency Patch For Critical Google Algorithm Flaw
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Issues Emergency Patch For Critical Google Algorithm Flaw
articles.content_orig:
A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library. The vulnerability affects multiple widely used technologies, including Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and more. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger memory corruption, disclose sensitive information, crash affected processes, or potentially achieve remote code execution (RCE).
Organizations using affected components to decompress untrusted Brotli-compressed data are advised to prioritize remediation.
CVE-2026-111497 was discovered and reported by Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer (OpenAI Codex Security), with fixes implemented by Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel (Node.js). Ron Masas (Imperva Red Team) demonstrated its exploitability, while OpenSourceMalware and Aikido analyzed its impact on the Python ecosystem.
Broccoli2Shell (a.k.a Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell) originates from an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, a widely adopted compression component used to reduce the size of HTTP traffic and other data. The flaw occurs when the decoder improperly handles specially crafted compressed data during block-processing operations, potentially writing beyond allocated memory boundaries. An attacker can exploit this behavior by supplying malicious Brotli-compressed input to a vulnerable application, potentially resulting in memory disclosure, application crashes, or arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected process. Researchers have demonstrated successful exploitation against unpatched Node.js environments.
Although initially associated with Node.js, the vulnerability originates in the upstream Brotli C decoder and extends to multiple downstream technologies that incorporate the affected component. Exploitation requires an application or dependency to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data, either through incoming HTTP requests, externally fetched responses, or other untrusted compressed content. Certain HTTP clients and application frameworks may perform decompression automatically when Brotli support is enabled, potentially exposing applications even when Brotli is not explicitly referenced in application code.
Cloud environments are particularly exposed due to the widespread use of Brotli-enabled components across containerized applications, Kubernetes clusters, API gateways, reverse proxies, serverless workloads, and cloud-hosted web services. Internet-facing applications that process attacker-controlled requests, as well as internal services that retrieve compressed responses from untrusted external sources, may provide exploitation paths. Successful exploitation could enable attackers to compromise application workloads, access sensitive information, disrupt service availability, or execute malicious code within affected containers or runtime environments.
According to Wiz data 91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497, and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances.
Additional products that bundle or link against vulnerable versions of the Brotli C decoder may also be affected. Organizations should consult vendor-specific security advisories, particularly for statically linked libraries and embedded dependencies. End-of-life runtime branches should be migrated to supported versions.
Organizations should prioritize the following mitigation and remediation measures:
Apply security updates: Upgrade affected Brotli libraries, Node.js runtimes, Python packages, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and Istio deployments to their respective patched versions or later supported releases.
Identify vulnerable cloud workloads: Inventory virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, containers, serverless functions, API gateways, and application dependencies for vulnerable Brotli components. Prioritize internet-facing services and workloads processing untrusted compressed data.
Review application exposure: Identify applications that decompress Brotli-compressed HTTP requests, external HTTP responses, uploaded files, or other attacker-controlled content. Include indirect and transitive dependencies in the assessment.
Rebuild and redeploy affected workloads: Update container base images, dependency lockfiles, and bundled libraries. Rebuild and redeploy affected container images, restart running processes, and verify that patched components are loaded.
Implement temporary mitigations: Where immediate patching is not possible, consider disabling Brotli decompression or rejecting Brotli-encoded requests before they reach vulnerable components. Restrict untrusted compressed responses where feasible. These controls may reduce exposure but do not replace patching.
Strengthen monitoring and detection: Review WAF, application, and network logs for suspicious Brotli-compressed traffic, unexpected application crashes, and anomalous process behavior. Monitor affected workloads for indicators of exploitation.
Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO filing reveals AI security breaches, training halt
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO filing reveals AI security breaches, training halt
articles.content_orig:
A cybersecurity test is supposed to measure what an AI model can do within an agreed boundary. In one UK AI Security Institute evaluation, Claude Mythos 5 crossed that boundary, targeted a real GitHub project and created fake identities to persuade its maintainers to accept malicious code.
The maintainers refused. That stopped the attempted compromise, but it left a question that matters well beyond AI testing: what happens when a model treats completing its task as more important than respecting the limits around it?
Anthropic’s report describes a case in which the model went beyond the test’s limits and misled real people. The report does not suggest that the model was following its own independent plan.
The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) gave Mythos 5 a cybersecurity challenge. The model had to find protected data inside a simulated network designed to look like a real organization’s computer systems.
Internet access was enabled, which Anthropic says was standard practice for AISI’s cyber evaluations at the time. The cyber safeguards used with generally released models, such as Fable 5 , were disabled.
Those conditions matter when interpreting the incident. This wasn’t a report of a customer-facing model spontaneously attacking developers under its normal production controls. Still, the consequences weren’t confined to the test.
“The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations.” reads the report published by Anthropic.
Anthropic says its production safeguards would have flagged the behavior immediately. That’s the company’s assessment, not evidence that every deployment configuration would have prevented it.
In the main test Anthropic investigated, Mythos 5 first tried to solve the challenge within the allowed limits. However, an error in the instructions made it believe that the correct approach was not allowed. This made solving the task properly difficult or even impossible.
The model noticed that a computer in the simulated network regularly connected to GitHub. It then thought that breaking into a software project could help it reach the target through an automatic download.
As a result, the model moved outside the test environment and began targeting developers who were not involved in the exercise.
Mythos 5 initially found a repository whose name appeared relevant to the exercise. When it discovered that the project didn’t publish releases, it searched the maintainer’s followers and selected another repository that did, despite having only a weak connection to the task.
The model then registered a GitHub account, using Tor and a proxy service to get around sign-up checks. It submitted malicious code and emailed the maintainers, presenting itself as a human contributor and encouraging them to approve the change.
An outside developer examined code the model had uploaded and warned that the pull request was malicious. Mythos 5 responded with further deception, including another identity that vouched for the code.
” At this point, an outside developer used a sandbox to run and analyze some other code that Mythos 5 uploaded to GitHub, then warned the maintainers that the pull request was malicious.” continues the report. “Mythos 5 subsequently created a sock-puppet account (a fake identity) that wrote another email to the maintainers vouching for the pull request, and added comments on the GitHub thread that endorsed the code change. The pull request was not accepted. “
The maintainers didn’t accept the pull request. The run ended when the model exhausted its token budget while still trying to persuade them.
Code review, in this case, did more than check the code. It held the boundary the evaluation hadn’t enforced.[ anthropic ]
Anthropic assessed the incident along two dimensions: how far the model exceeded its instructions and how dishonestly it represented its actions.
Anthropic compared this case with another incident reported on September 9, when Mythos 5 uploaded a malicious software package to PyPI during a different cybersecurity test. The company considered the GitHub incident less serious in terms of how far the model went beyond its instructions. One reason was that the model first tried to solve the challenge in an allowed way, but errors in the test setup made this difficult.
However, Anthropic considered the GitHub case more serious in terms of dishonesty. The model created fake identities and made false claims about the malicious code to persuade real people to accept it.
Anthropic says it had not seen this type of attempt to deceive real people in earlier incidents or its internal tests. Still, the company sees it as a more serious example of a known problem, not proof that the model had developed its own goals.
This distinction matters. An AI system does not need to have its own ambitions to cause harm. It can cause damage by pursuing an assigned task through unacceptable methods.
Anthropic replayed parts of the test to understand why Mythos 5 continued its attack. Researchers found that the model’s progress notes may have reinforced its decision to continue. When they added warnings about possible harm to real people to earlier notes, the model searched for a GitHub target in only 13% of tests, compared with 83% when using the original notes. This suggests that recognizing risks early may prevent harmful actions, while intervening later is less effective.
In further tests, Mythos 5 continued the attack in 98% of cases. Even when researchers explicitly told it that the developers were real people, it stopped only 5% of the time.
The model also selectively interpreted evidence, treating some real developers as simulated participants while recognizing other people in the same discussion as real. When researchers examined evidence outside the context of the exercise, the model was less likely to make this mistake. Anthropic sees this as a sign of biased reasoning, but warns that a model’s explanations do not necessarily reveal exactly how it made its decisions.
Mythos 5 was still able to change its approach. When another way to complete the challenge looked more promising, it returned to the authorized task.
Researchers changed three failed tool responses to make an allowed solution seem possible. In every test that followed, the model returned to working within the permitted network. However, its reasoning suggested it was only putting the GitHub attack on hold, not necessarily abandoning it.
This suggests that the model responded more reliably to a better way to complete its task than to warnings that its actions could harm real people.
Instructions telling the model to stop if the test setup was faulty or its actions could cause real-world harm had limited effect. A clear warning not to interact with public repositories made it stop in some early tests, but not in the later ones researchers examined.
Anthropic tested the same scenarios with Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5 and a more advanced internal model. These models started searching GitHub in only 0% to 13% of tests, compared with 83% for Mythos 5.
Stopping an attack already in progress was harder. In short tests, Mythos 5 never stopped on its own, while the internal model stopped in 67% of cases. Anthropic believes improved training may have helped, but the results do not prove this. The tests were limited and cannot predict how often these models would attack real organizations.
Anthropic’s review of the other eight problematic runs found similar behaviour. Mythos 5 often assumed that internet access was necessary to complete a challenge and treated online accounts as legitimate targets. Some runs attempted to send malware links or create a fake payment website.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The team over at the Nasdaq is having one hell of a week.
General Motors ( GM ) said on Tuesday it will transfer the listing of its common stock to the Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17.
The decision likely reflects GM trying to emphasize its tech bona-fides such as surging recurring revenue for Super Cruise.
It comes not too long after fellow Corporate America icon Walmart ( WMT ) — with its own growth oriented tech story to tell investors — switched to the Nasdaq from the NYSE in December 2025.
The news from GM is less than 24 hours removed from Anthropic selecting Nasdaq for its historic IPO listing, which is expected to take place by mid-November.

The card’s annual fee will be increasing to $150, though the card will also be getting all kinds of new benefits . Here are the new benefits being added to the Citi AAdvantage Business Card:

While these changes apply effective immediately for new applicants, existing cardmembers won’t immediately see the changes. Beginning January 24, 2027, existing cardmembers (on both the personal and business card) will have access to the new benefits. They’ll also be billed the new $150 annual fee on their next account anniversary after that date.
Essentially we’re seeing the annual fees on American’s two mid-range cards increase by $51 per year, and I’d say we’re seeing three primary improvements. Those include a $100 annual inflight credit, a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit every four years, and much better travel coverage.
Obviously I’m not a fan of credit card annual fee inflation, and of the general trend of cards with sub-$100 annual fees becoming more expensive.
However, I generally think that if you found either card worthwhile before, you’ll probably still find it worthwhile after. At the same time, I don’t necessarily think these changes will make the card materially more appealing for anyone. So I’d view these as being pretty balanced and reasonable changes, even though I wish we weren’t seeing a fee hike. Then again, the cards have had these same types of fees for years, so the price increase basically just matches inflation.
Random thought — with all the American cards adding new inflight credits, I sure wish American would actually improve its selection of drinks and snacks for purchase, including shortening the minimum length of flight for items to be for sale. Actually using these credits just isn’t easy at times.
American Airlines and Citi are making changes to their co-brand credit card portfolio, particularly impacting the Platinum and Business products. Both cards will be seeing annual fees increase from $99 to $150, while getting new perks, including new bonus categories on spending, a $100 annual inflight credit, a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit, and improved travel coverage.
I’d probably view these changes as broadly being “breakeven,” in terms of the overall value propositions. I’m not a fan of the fee increase, but I also don’t think the value proposition is getting worse here, assuming you’re someone who values either card as is.

articles.title_orig: China’s economy may never overtake America — and it’s all due to an ill-fated 47-year-old policy
articles.title_zh: China’s economy may never overtake America — and it’s all due to an ill-fated 47-year-old policy
articles.content_orig:
Just one child doomed China’s hopes of overtaking the US.
The Middle Kingdom, once a surging economic growth engine expected to eclipse the US economy in just a few years, is not expected to outgrow the US until the 2040s now — if it does at all.
And it’s largely down to China’s 1979 One Child Policy , which is devastating growth, according to Yi Fuxian, a Chinese demographer at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
Plummeting birth rates and economic problems have erased the 6+% per year growth that China reported before the COVID-19 pandemic.
Many economists in both China and the West were taken in by the Chinese Communist Party’s inflated official figures, which massively overestimated the country’s consumer power, Fuxian said.
It comes as a Goldman Sachs study found that China’s population began shrinking in 2022 , just 13 years after that of neighboring Japan. And its decline is on track to be far steeper, dramatically damaging the country’s economic prospects, the Financial Times reported .
China has a GDP of $21.6 trillion — just two-thirds the size of the US economy.
Yi told The Post that official Chinese statistics have systematically inflated the country’s birthrates and total population figures going back decades.
While official reports claim China has a population of over 1.4 billion, Yi calculates that the true figure in 2020 was “under 1.28 billion,” at least 130 million lower than reported.
India actually surpassed China as the world’s most populous nation years earlier than officially recognized, according to Yi, author of the 2007 book, “Big Country with an Empty Nest,” which criticized China’s one-child policies.
The US, the third most populous country in the world, has 342 million people — about a quarter the population of China.
Yi argues that China’s population actually began shrinking in 2018, four years earlier than Goldman Sachs’ estimate, and more than a decade before the official projection of 2031 to 2034.
Most of this can be attributed to China’s notorious One Child Policy , instituted to limit Chinese families to one child per mother, over fears of spiraling population growth and widespread poverty.
While the policy was relaxed to two children per couple in 2016 and three children in 2021, China’s total fertility rate remains one of the lowest in the world .
China is no longer poor — officially 0% of the population is in extreme poverty, compared to 88% 40 years ago.
But it’s also not rich; the per capita GDP is about $13,800 per year, about 15% of that in the US.
Turkey, Russia and Kazakhstan are all richer than China by that measure.
The country’s total fertility rate fell below the 2.1 replacement level in 1991 and continued to plummet, dropping below 1.0 and now estimated to be just 0.8 births per woman, according to Yi.
Last year saw a record low of just 8 million live births in China. The much smaller US, by contrast, had 3.6 million births.
Yi also blames the economic reforms of China’s former Premier Zhu Rongji in the 1990s, for causing “many problems” that slowed down China’s economic growth and race to catch up with the US.
Decades of strict birth restrictions and fiscal centralization severely curtailed household disposable income in China, to roughly 42-44% of GDP.
In contrast, in the US, that figure is over 70% of GDP.
While this may have helped China’s economy in the short term, allowing it to flood the US with cheap imported goods, in the long run, it may have signed the CCP’s suicide note, according to Yi.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
Children function as “super-consumers,” driving much of household spending, he explained.
With China missing several full generations worth of children, this severely crippled Chinese domestic consumption, he argued.
To offset weak domestic consumption, China became heavily dependent on manufacturing exports, an unsustainable real estate bubble, and state-subsidized industrial overcapacity, he explained.
Those policies, “killed China’s economy, the population and the economy — and also killed America’s manufacturing,” Yi said.
China is now one of the oldest countries in the world, with a rapidly shrinking labor pool and aging population. The median age is expected to reach 59 by 2050, compared to 44 in the US.
This means Beijing may never catch up with the US economically — and worse, could face a long-term economic deceleration, Yi argued.
Yi puts the over-optimistic predictions about China’s economic growth down to mainstream economists and Chinese government-aligned institutions relying on fabricated data — assuming China’s population would soon grow five times larger than the US.
This played into the popular narrative that “the East is rising while the West is declining,” he said, while the truth is very different.
“By 2029 to 2035, China will lag behind the US across all major demographic and growth metrics,” Yi said.
However, for pro-democracy activists who might hope that this demographic time bomb could topple the CCP, Yi has a warning.
Contrary to Western expectations that economic development would foster a pro-democracy middle class, China’s rapid aging has depleted it of the young population required to drive political activism.
Just 16% of China is aged 15 to 29, down from 31% at the time of China’s last mass-democracy movement in 1989, which culminated in the communists’ brutal crackdown in Tiananmen Square.
An aging, risk-averse China is far more likely to support a centralized strongman who will safeguard pensions and social stability, Yi explained.

articles.title_orig: Boeing narrows third-quarter loss as defense sales rise, but focus remains on 737 Max production
articles.title_zh: Boeing narrows third-quarter loss as defense sales rise, but focus remains on 737 Max production
articles.content_orig:
Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.
CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected becuase of the wings production pace.
Boeing stock was down about 9% during the call.
"I know everybody wants us to go faster but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.
Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

articles.title_orig: China’s fifth plenum focuses on discipline and loyalty to Xi
articles.title_zh: China’s fifth plenum focuses on discipline and loyalty to Xi
articles.content_orig:
Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy â branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" â to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September,  the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

articles.title_orig: GM will switch to Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17
articles.title_zh: GM will switch to Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — General Motors plans to transfer shares of its common stock from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq as the automaker attempts to position itself more as a technology-focused company.
The Detroit automaker said Tuesday that it expects to begin trading as a Nasdaq -listed company on Nov. 17. Its ticker symbol is expected to remain "GM," the company said.
"GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," GM CFO Paul Jacobson said in a release. "We're grateful for our long-standing partnership with the New York Stock Exchange and its remarkable legacy."
GM noted the move will provide eligibility for potential inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 Index .
Current shareholders do not need to take any action with respect to the transfer, the company said.
The switch marks a notable loss for the NYSE, as GM first listed on the exchange in 1911. The Detroit automaker also relisted on the stock exchange in 2010 following a government-backed bankruptcy.
GM follows other companies such as Walmart , DoorDash and Palantir Technologies that have transferred from the more traditional NYSE to the historically technology focused Nasdaq in recent years. Hilton Worldwide Holdings last week also announced plans to move trading from the NYSE to Nasdaq.
The key drivers for a listing transfer differ from company to company, but the Nasdaq in 2024 said common reasons include "index inclusion opportunities, cost effective fee structure, brand visibility partnership, access to Nasdaq's event space, and Nasdaq's suite of investor relations and ESG products."
GM's decision comes a week after the automaker held a technology-focused event where executives laid out the company's roadmap for artificial intelligence and self-driving vehicle technologies.
Shares of GM, which has been aggressively buying back stock , have more than doubled since 2024. GM's stock closed Monday at $76.31 per share. The company's market cap is roughly $64.4 billion.

articles.title_orig: Man charged with assisting ‘foreign intelligence service’ after incident at UK base used for Iran strikes
articles.title_zh: Man charged with assisting ‘foreign intelligence service’ after incident at UK base used for Iran strikes
articles.content_orig:
The U.K. has said it had charged a man with an offense of assisting a "foreign intelligence service" over an incident at a military base used by the U.S. for strikes on Iran.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, has been charged under the country's National Security Act "following an incident involving RAF Fairford," an air base in west England, prosecutors announced on Tuesday .
Between Aug. 31 and Sept. 28, Abdulkarim is alleged to have engaged in "conduct that would likely materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities", the Crown Prosecution Service added. The foreign country was not named.
Prosecutors also charged 24-year-old Nouman Essghir with "entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK".
The men are due to appear in court in London on Tuesday.
Five people were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses near RAF Fairford on Sept. 28. The base had been used as the U.S. Air Force's command outpost for operations from Europe and for American strikes on Iranian missile sites.
Announcing the charges, Frank Ferguson, a chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said that they followed "a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford."
"We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues," he said.
After the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. had moved its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to a threat "linked to Iran."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers earlier this month that the incident was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."
Over the summer, Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned it saw any military base involved in launching airstrikes on Iran as a legitimate target.
Tehran denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

articles.title_orig: Two British Men Charged Over Major Security Incident at U.K. Air Base
articles.title_zh: Two British Men Charged Over Major Security Incident at U.K. Air Base
articles.content_orig:
Oct. 27 (UPI) -- Authorities in Britain on Tuesday charged a 24-year-old man with spying for a foreign intelligence service, allegedly Iran, in relation to an incident at RAF Fairford in September in which a group of masked men in vans were arrested by counter-terrorism police near the base in the middle of the night.
The Crown Prosecution Service said in a news release that Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim of London was charged under the National Security Act with assisting a foreign intelligence service by carrying out activities in Britain between Aug. 31 and Sept. 28 "likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service."
"In this case, we believe that country to be Iran ," said Head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor.
A second man, Nouman Essghir, 24 and also from London, was charged with a single National Security offense that on Aug. 22 he entered, scoped out or got too close to a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men are due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court later on Tuesday.
Five others arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses during the alleged Sept. 27 incident in the Gloucestershire village of Whelford, a half mile from the base, and then re-arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, are free on police bail, Counter Terrorism Policing said.
CTP added that an eighth man, a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national who was re-arrested last week, has been released without charge but remains on strict police bail.
"We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the Director General of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat," said CTP Assistant Commissioner Taylor.
RAF Fairford had been used by the U.S. military to fly missions amid its war with Iran.
A week after the security incident, the United States pulled out all of its bomber aircraft -- at least a dozen long-range B-1s -- stationed at the base, citing "threats."

articles.title_orig: Asian Stocks to Gain as Anthropic Files for IPO: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Asian Stocks to Gain as Anthropic Files for IPO: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
The tech industry needs this to go well. So does Wall Street.
Anthropic's IPO filing on Monday puts the Claude creator in position to pursue what could be the largest initial stock offering in history. Investors are already measuring the 5-year-old company's potential market cap in the trillions, putting it in a category with the world's most valuable companies.
It's a critical moment for the whole tech sector, as the artificial intelligence boom has been largely driven by two companies: Anthropic and OpenAI. The latter has confidentially filed to go public, but has said a debut likely won't take place until 2027.
Meanwhile, the stock market is showing signs of jitters on the AI trade. Neoclouds and data center companies have been getting pummeled, prompting Australia's Firmus to withdraw its IPO plans and for SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm unit to do the same.
Now, all eyes turn to Anthropic , which is betting that investors will look past over $80 billion in losses in the first half of the year, and see the 14-fold increase in revenue as a reflection of seemingly insatiable demand for the company's leading models and services.
"If it underperforms expectations, it'll be a little bit of a house of cards," said Jai Das, co-founder of Sapphire Ventures whose career in tech investing dates to the 1990s.
Anthropic's business is deeply entwined with tech megacaps. Close to half its revenue comes from Claude being sold through cloud divisions at Microsoft , Amazon and Alphabet , which all hold investments in the company. In the IPO, some $77 billion in notes can be issued to Amazon , Broadcom and Google , while Microsoft and Nvidia agreed to invest $15 billion as the company builds up its computing capacity. Chips from Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices , Amazon and Google are powering Anthropic's development.
Cloud providers are ratcheting up capital expenditures to meet demand, and memory manufacturers are fighting shortages to prioritize AI chips. And there's the debt factor. Alphabet, with its investment-grade credit rating, committed to backstopping Anthropic for a data center in Texas. Broadcom , which helps Google develop chips for AI labs, is creating financing pools to help Anthropic and OpenAI deploy high-performance models, CEO Hock Tan told analysts earlier this year.
For public market investors, more than one-third of the value of the S&P 500 comes from tech's trillion-dollar companies, which are all, to varying degrees, going deep in AI. Beyond that, there are software giants like Adobe and Salesforce that have integrated with Anthropic's Claude assistant.
And in the private markets, check sizes have ballooned but IPOs are few and far between. Bessemer Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures both told CNBC that Anthropic is their biggest investment ever.
"If they don't perform well, they will become the bellwether for AI," said Brad Bernstein, a managing partner at growth equity firm FTV Capital. "Their valuation will reflect that performance variation, and then it'll just be a trickle-down effect to all the stuff going on with the excess capital that's getting poured into the venture AI world. Everything is going to have to sort of be reset."
Anthropic will be the third company to go public with a valuation above $1 trillion, after Saudi Aramco and Elon Musk's SpaceX , which debuted in June. OpenAI could be the fourth.
Revenue at Anthropic has been multiplying at a staggering pace as businesses adopt the company's coding and productivity tools. Second-quarter revenue soared to $11.56 billion from $787 million a year earlier.
The company held almost $132 billion in cash, equivalents and short-term investments at the end of June. And after five quarters of operating losses, Anthropic reported $974 million in operating income for the second quarter.
"It is, I think, better than feared," said Rohit Kulkarni, partner and chief AI officer at Burnham Park Capital Markets, referring to the financials. "There could have been more negative tidbits."
One source of concern in some corners of the investing universe is the emergence of so-called open-weight models, which are cheaper for businesses to access and allow for customization and flexibility in terms of where users access the models.
In the prospectus, the only two competitors Anthropic named were OpenAI and Google, though the company said it faces competition from a "broader set of model providers," including open-weight or open-source models.
Anthropic says it's all very early, with Fortune 500 companies committing less than 0.1% of their total expenses to its models and services in the latest quarter. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs, says that's part of the investment thesis.
"I think there's going to be room for frontier models like Anthropic and OpenAI and SpaceX, and I think there will be room for open-weight models," Monaghan said. "It's way too soon to say that one is going to disintermediate the other."
With hyperscaler spending on AI infrastructure set to reach into the trillions of dollars, Sapphire's Das said there's understandable concern about a market glut. But he compares it to the telecommunications and dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when companies flooded the market with fiber-optic equipment. Eventually, the infrastructure got used, although plenty of companies went belly up in the interim.
"Long term, I don't think there is a lack of demand," Das said.
A lackluster debut could push out OpenAI's offering even further and cause investors to rethink its lofty valuation. At the same time, rising interest rates mean it's getting costlier for companies to raise debt.
David Trainer, CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, wrote in a report last month that the AI boom has been built on the view that cheap credit and access to the capital markets will be "readily available."
"If AI liquidity dries up, and there are clear signs it is, we see large, 20%, downside risk in the S&P 500, with most of that concentrated in the valuation of AI-related stocks," Trainer wrote.
Industry experts take a different approach, focusing on the power and rapid proliferation of the technology. Claude Opus 5.5 Max performs better than any other model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an industry benchmark .
Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy said the technology is only becoming more essential.
"Anthropic and OpenAI have by now demonstrated their ability to stay at the frontier of AI and keep pushing innovation," Ramaswamy said. "They're incredible companies that are doing a big service to humanity by expanding the frontier of what is possible, and we are very much rooting for them to be public and very successful companies."
Still, Snowflake is experimenting with low-cost open-weight models from China's Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and Zhipu.
"We spend a lot on internal AI because we want to get as much efficiency as we can," Ramaswamy said.

articles.title_orig: Porsche profit rebounds as luxury carmaker reduces exposure to China
articles.title_zh: Porsche profit rebounds as luxury carmaker reduces exposure to China
articles.content_orig:
German sports carmaker Porsche said it has significantly reduced its exposure to China as operating profit rebounded in the first nine months of the year despite falling revenue and vehicle deliveries.
The Volkswagen-owned company published its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, announcing that operating profit was 1.74 billion euros ($1.94 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 40 million euros at the same time last year, when it booked around 2.7 billion euros in strategic restructuring costs.
Meanwhile, sales revenue fell 5.9% to 25.28 billion euros, while deliveries continued to decline, down 16% to 178,532. North America remained Porsche's largest sales region by volume.
China has historically been an important market for German luxury automakers, but they have struggled with growing competition from domestic brands, particularly in electric vehicles.
Porsche's China sales have fallen sharply in recent years amid intensifying competition from brands such as BYD, Geely and Xiaomi.
"Our geographically balanced sales footprint continues to provide resilience across different markets," Jochen Breckner, Porsche's chief financial officer, said in the earnings webcast on Tuesday.
"As you know, we have significantly reduced our exposure to China. This makes our overall business less dependent on developments from this challenging market environment."
Porsche shares were last seen trading 2.3% higher.
Porsche is also cutting thousands of jobs as part of a broader restructuring aimed at reducing costs and responding to weaker demand.
Citi analysts said in a note Tuesday that Porsche's first-nine-month results were as expected, despite challenges including China.
"Despite challenging conditions, including exceptionally low deliveries, higher costs, and higher battery electric vehicle deliveries, Porsche's underlying EBIT remains very resilient and ahead of German premium peers," the analysts said.
They added that Porsche has laid out a plan to return to double-digit underlying operating profit margins, with recovery expected to start in 2028, and net cash flow expected to rebound to above its IPO levels by 2031.
"Whilst FY27 will remain a trough year, we still see a solid, well-supported and credible multi-year EBIT and net cash recovery starting financial year 2028 - unlike many peers," the analysts said.

articles.title_orig: China's economy is outpacing the US despite Trump's tariffs. Here's what JPMorgan says it could mean for your money
articles.title_zh: China's economy is outpacing the US despite Trump's tariffs. Here's what JPMorgan says it could mean for your money
articles.content_orig:
Voting booths are seen at Supervisor of Elections Office in Orange County, Florida, on the last business day before early voting begins for the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm elections.
William Diaz has a mantra: His only political party is his Venezuelan community.
He doesn’t abide by strict partisan rules, and doesn't believe in only voting for Democrats or Republicans. He supported Republicans Sen. Rick Scott and Secretary of State Marco Rubio when they were running for office in Florida , where Diaz has lived for 37 years.
For these midterm elections, however, the Orlando resident hopes to make a clear statement: He does not support President Donald Trump’s immigration policies and is unhappy with how Republican-backed initiatives have affected his community.
Read More: An Idaho ICE Raid Rounded Up Hundreds. The Fallout Could Change How ICE Operates
“I voted already, and what I did when I was voting and when I was with my ballot, I was really thinking and praying for all those that has no voice, those that can not vote, those immigrants that are right now victim of actions on the streets,” Diaz tells TIME, referring to Trump’s mass deportation agenda and the expansive influence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). “My people have been suffering that much.”
Diaz is one of more than 2.6 million people who have already cast ballots in Florida, either by mail or through in-person early voting, according to state figures released Sunday. In-person early voting began in some counties Oct. 19 and expanded statewide Oct. 24.
Diaz’s community is one part of a Florida Latino electorate with varied national origins and political loyalties. Taken together, however, Latino voters are a swing vote in several closely watched races statewide. They were key to Trump’s Florida victory in 2024, with 56% supporting him over Kamala Harris, according to the 2024 American Electorate Voter Poll .
But new polls ahead of Election Day suggest that Latino support for the GOP may be on shaky ground—a shift that could put Republicans to the test in Florida and shape the political landscape beyond November.
Dissatisfaction among Florida’s Latino voters reflects a broader national mood, according to Stephanie Valencia, a co-founder of Equis Research, an organization that studies Latino voting behavior.
Concerns about the economy and immigration enforcement tactics are fueling dissatisfaction among Latino voters, who “make up a huge part of the electorate in Florida,” she says, pointing out that both of these issues are “disproportionately impacting” them.
A Univision/YouGov poll, conducted Oct. 2–15, showed that 41% of registered Latino voters in Florida were “very or somewhat worried” that they, a family member, or someone close could be detained or otherwise directly affected by immigration enforcement, compared with 27% of Florida voters overall.
The same poll showed that 4 in 10 Latino voters in the state felt that their finances had worsened over the past year, with 70% disapproving of Trump’s handling of the cost of living in the U.S. That stands in comparison to a 63% disapproval rate from Florida voters overall.
Read More: Midterm Ad Spending Has Surpassed $10B. Where Is the Money Coming From?
For Johanna Chavez, a Dominican immigrant living in Kissimmee, Florida, the economy is top of mind.
“Many people are concerned about the economy and the price of gasoline … and then there’s the cost of rent, it’s become incredibly, overwhelmingly high,” Chavez, who speaks Spanish, tells TIME through a translator. “All the things they promised would be done—nothing has happened.”
In the past few years, Chavez says it has felt like the United States has started “regressing,” and the opportunities she was looking for when she arrived here have not materialized in the way she had hoped.
“It’s starting to feel just like the situation back in my home country, the Dominican Republic,” she says. “We all came here hoping for change, seeking a better life, but it’s ending up being the same thing all over again. Things just aren’t what they’re supposed to be.”
Jared Nordlund, the Florida State Advocacy Director at UnidosUS, the largest nonprofit Latino rights organization in the U.S., says this is a common refrain among Floridian Latinos; people are upset over how the economy has been affected by tariffs and the war in Iran . Florida was hit particularly hard by rising gas prices after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz squeezed the global energy supply, he says.
“Florida is not a state friendly for public transportation, so people are highly reliant on the cars, and so what they would be paying for food now is having to kind of get broke between … paying to get the gas and then going to get food,” Nordlund says.
The question now is whether that dissatisfaction will translate into votes against Republicans—and whether it will be enough to tip the state’s close races.
Trump’s approval rating has plummeted with Latino voters in Florida, dropping from 58% approval at the start of his term to 36% ahead of midterm elections, according to Equis Research.
According to an AP-NORC poll from October, about 6 in 10 Latino voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency, and more than 7 in 10 disapprove of how he is handling the economy.
A Pew Research Center poll found that Trump’s job approval rating among Latino voters dropped from 38% in February 2025 to 24% in September and October. Of those who backed him in the last election, approval dropped to 57%—down from 93% in early 2025.
The shift may be resonating with Republicans like Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who is seeking re-election in Florida’s 27th District in Miami-Dade—a majority Latino district that Trump carried by some 15 points in 2024. She publicly broke with Trump in her campaign and criticized his immigration policies.
In one ad in September, Salazar said that Trump has “gone too far" with his deportation agenda.
“In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record,” she notes in the ad.
“Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” Salazar continues, addressing Trump. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
Guillermo Grenier, a Cuban American professor of sociology at Florida International University (FIU), agrees that many Latino voters are “ticked off” at Trump.
“The population, if you look at the whole Latino conglomerate, is turned off pretty strongly with Trump,” he says.
But South Florida’s Latino electorate is unique; Grenier points out that the state is home to 1.9 million Cuban Americans—the largest concentration in the United States.
As a voting bloc, the community has significant sway. In 2024, FIU’s Cuba poll found that 68% of likely Cuban American voters in Miami-Dade County supported Trump, compared to 23% for Harris—representing his highest-recorded support level in the poll's history.
A shift away from Republicans among Cuban American voters could therefore have significant consequences in South Florida. But disillusionment doesn’t always turn into action, according to Grenier.
“I think a lot of Cubans are pissed off at Trump, but they're still Republicans,” he says.
The Democratic Party’s response to this potential opening may unfold over several election cycles.
“Democrats are going to be in a probationary period with Latinos and with all voters, quite frankly, on whether they can deliver or not,” Valencia says. “One election is not durable support among a particular group.”
The electorate’s age also matters to its long-term political influence, says Michael McDonald, a professor of political science at the University of Florida. “Latinos are much younger than the rest of the population in the United States.”
He points out that voter turnout “is highly correlated with age” and expects Latino participation to increase as younger voters grow older. In his assessment, that could reshape the electoral map beyond

articles.title_zh: Here's the cash windfall the Anthropic IPO may bring to banks like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
It stands to be a bountiful holiday quarter for some of the world's biggest banks, courtesy of the gift-giving team at Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ).
Using the SpaceX IPO fee rate, allocations, and a range of potential proceeds, EvercoreISI analyst Glenn Schorr estimates Anthropic's offering could generate a roughly $562 million equity capital markets (ECM) fee pool. That would equal about 1% of fourth-quarter consensus EPS across the banks he covers.
In Schorr's base case, co-lead underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley would each haul in $112 million in fees. Bank of America, Citigroup, and JPMorgan would each rake in $84 million.
A total of 22 banks appear on Anthropic's IPO tombstone, an advertisement recognizing the investment banks and other financial firms helping take the company public.
"A successful listing could also encourage more AI companies to test the public markets, accelerate broader IPO momentum, and reinforce the view that the AI trade still has room to run," Schorr added.
Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus shows. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.
Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.
Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November.
"I think this needs to be valued appropriately," Manhattan Ventures co-founder Jare Carmel said on Sozzi Unleashed . Manhattan Venture Partners is an investor in Anthropic. "I think the biggest problem that we've seen in the IPO markets over the last few years are sort of valuations that have been offsides. And this needs to be valued to sell the IPO buyer, whether that's institutional or retail. They seem to hop around, especially when they're not getting the pop that they need. And I can fully understand why a company like Anthropic wouldn't would want to value themselves fairly as opposed to, let's say, undervalued. But the reality is you need to have shareholders for the long term."
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title_orig: Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
articles.title_zh: Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
articles.content_orig:
Israelis are voting in a closely watched election to decide on the direction of the country, three years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on southern Israel that set off the genocidal war on Gaza.
The first election since those attacks comes at a time when Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of its neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.
But the vote also comes amid growing domestic questions that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces over alleged failures that allowed the October 7 attack, his government’s handling of efforts to retrieve captives taken to Gaza, alleged corruption and disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service .
In final polls published Friday, Netanyahu’s coalition is expected to be neck and neck with – or trail slightly behind – the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
According to Israeli news outlet Haaretz, which has collated polls from Israeli news channels, as of Friday, an average of Channels 11, 12 and 13 predicts Netanyahu’s bloc will win 50 seats while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc will take 54 seats. The Israeli parliament, known as the Knesset, has 120 seats in all, so 61 is the mark that a grouping needs to reach a majority.
Here’s what you need to know about the election.
On Tuesday, polls opened at 7am local time (05:00 GMT) and will end at 10pm (20:00 GMT).
About 7.3 million Israelis will be eligible to vote, including 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel. Israelis living abroad cannot vote because the country does not have a general absentee ballot, requiring voters to be physically present on election day.
Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception and cast their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.
News channels will broadcast exit poll results once the election ends, with the first indications likely within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or weeks to get a clear result.
Results will also be live on the Central Elections Committee website once polls close.
While a clear picture of the election results may come out quickly, if no party or coalition secures a majority, it could take much longer.
The final vote tally is expected by Friday, and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.
Under a proportional representation system, Israelis vote for a single party, not individual candidates.
The number of seats the party gains in the Knesset is linked to the proportion of the vote it receives. For example, if Netanyahu’s Likud party secures 50 percent of the national vote, it would take 50 percent of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats.
For a party to enter the Knesset, it must secure at least 3.25 percent of the national vote.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
Once the final count is in, President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
The person nominated then has up to 42 days to form a government. As it stands, no single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks.
If no government emerges, the current cabinet, Netanyahu’s government, will remain as a caretaker government.
But before that point, whoever gains the most votes will have different options to assemble support from smaller parties, including forming a minority government or working with another political leader to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.
If all negotiations fail, and no grouping is able to cobble together a workable government, new elections will have to be called.

articles.title_zh: Israelis head to polls in first election since the October 7 Hamas-led terror attack
articles.content_orig:
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:
Voter turnout in the first three hours of the Israeli general election was the highest in decades, Israel 's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday.
According to the committee, nationwide turnout by mid-morning was already at 16.68%, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981 and up from 15.9% at the same time in the 2022 election.
"By 10 a.m., more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted," said the committee's acting director general, Dean Livne.
Total voter turnout in Israeli general elections approached 80% the 1990s but hasn't been higher than 72.3% since the turn of the century. Turnout at the last general election in 2022 was 70.6%.
Turnout among Arab Israelis is expected to be particularly important given the role Arab parties could play as potential kingmakers in coalition talks.
"Our vote will change the government," predicted Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party as he cast his vote, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.
Arabs in Israel make up about 18% of the electorate, and pre-election surveys have suggested a sharp increase in voter participation.
Data from the Midgam Research Institute cited by the Qatar -owned The New Arab indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in previous elections. The National , based in the United Arab Emirates , said its sources were predicting an "astronomical" Arab turnout.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Around 7.3 million Israelis (including around 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel) are eligible to vote on Tuesday.
More than 640,000 young Israelis will be eligible to vote in a general election for the first time.
Around 3.1 million Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank do not have the right to vote in Israeli elections, but 500,000 illegal settlers in those territories do.
A further 350,000 Palestinians live in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and also cannot vote, whereas around 230,000 Israelis living there can.
The US-based non-profit America-Israel Democracy Coalition (AID Coalition) has organized a "Fly&Vote" initiative, with as many as 67,000 voters returning to Israel to participate in the election, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data.
The coalition said half are coming from the US, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Israel does not have postal voting.
Israel is a parliamentary democracy and voters elect a legislature rather than choosing their prime minister directly. Voters choose a party "list."
Israel uses a proportional representation system under which 120 parliamentary seats are distributed roughly in proportion to a party's share of the vote.
To enter parliament (known as the Knesset), parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes, which is equivalent to roughly four seats.
The party which can command a majority of at least 61 seats is called upon to form a government. No single party has ever won an outright majority, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Polls suggest this year will be no different.
Unlike many other democracies around the world, Israel is not divided up into geographic electoral districts.
Rather than electing individual lawmakers to represent local areas, voters in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and Haifa all choose from the same party lists in one, single, nationwide constituency.
When polling stations close at 10 p.m. local time (9 p.m. CET), broadcasters will publish their first exit polls, offering an initial indication of the results. Official results are scheduled to be published on November 4.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
While the main competition for the largest number of seats is between Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the Arab parties are projected to play a key role in determining Israel's next ruling coalition.
For a party or coalition to rule, it needs to secure 61 seats in the Knesset.
As per a recent Channel 12 poll, Eisenkot's bloc is hovering around 55 seats, while Netanyahu's bloc is trailing behind with some 51 seats. This means that either bloc would need to form coalitions in order to rule, should the election results come out similar to the polls.
The most likely parties to tip the scales are the Joint List (projected to win around 9 seats) and the Ra'am (projected to win around 5 seats). The Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by nationality, make up around a fifth of Israel's eligible voters. Polls suggest a higher turnout rate for the Arab voters than seen in previous elections.
Netanyahu's Likud and Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudi parties attempted last month to ban the Joint List and Ra'am from running in the race, but Israel's Supreme Court reversed the parties' disqualification earlier in October.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties. But analysts suggest such stances are not set in stone and can shift amid coalition talks, a move Netanyahu himself has resorted to in the past.
The Israeli general election is considered by many to be a verdict on the country's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu .
But who is the opposition, and what do they stand for?
The main opposition force is a so-called "change bloc," a mixed group of center-right and some left-wing parties led by the newly formed Yashar (honesty) party and its leader Gadi Eisenkot.
A relative political newcomer, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to become the chief of the staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) between 2015 and 2019.
Eisenkot has positioned himself squarely in opposition to Netanyahu in terms of his personality — an unpolished man of the people in contrast to the highly stylized and controlling prime minister.
Campaigning on accountability, political reform, and national unity, Eisenkot has sharply criticized Netanyahu's leadership before and after the October 7 Hamas attacks.
But his politics don't differ massively and, although he has emphasized equal rights for all Israeli citizens, he has been ambiguous on the idea of a two-state solution since October 7.
While backing Israel's military operations, he argues the government lacks a clear strategy and has called for an independent inquiry into the failures surrounding the attacks. His military record and the death of his son in the Gaza war have strengthened his standing among many voters
The parties in Eisenkot's bloc all have ideological differences but are united by their goal of removing Netanyahu from power.

Voting began in Israel at 7 a.m. local time (6 a.m. CET) on Tuesday in the first general election since the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the devastating war in Gaza unleashed by Israel in response.
Some 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote, with polls showing a bloc led by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , the country's longest-serving premier, neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot's centrist opposition alliance.
Most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. local time (8 p.m. UTC).
There's a lot at stake in this election: The fallout and questions of political accountability for the attacks of October 7, 2023; mandatory military service for ultra-Orthodox men and sharing the burden of national defense; along with Israel's standing in the international community.
Nowhere can the division within Israeli society be more felt than in debate over Benjamin Netanyahu .
