articles.title_orig: Deadly Russian ballistic missile attack hits Kyiv university, bridge, medical centers
articles.title_zh: Deadly Russian ballistic missile attack hits Kyiv university, bridge, medical centers
articles.content_orig:
Help us keep bringing the truth to light, even when Russia turns the lights out.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a deadly attack overnight on Oct. 26-27, striking a university campus, a major bridge, an administrative building, and medical facilities.
Kyiv, a city of three million people, has been relentlessly assaulted by Russian ballistic missiles in recent months as Moscow exploits Ukraine's air defense shortage. While its battlefield offensive has slowed, Russia has chosen a strategy of mass aerial strikes against vulnerable civilians.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people have been injured in the latest Russian attack , Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Those injured in the attack include a paramedic, a medical technician, and a 20-year-old university student.
The mayor later reported a strike on the city's Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River, one of Kyiv's major traffic arteries. The bridge connects the city's eastern and western sides and is crucial for the daily commutes of hundreds of thousands of residents.
The bridge and metro infrastructure were damaged overnight, Klitschko said. Train service on the bridge has been temporarily suspended.
Ihor, who lives on the east bank of the Dnipro River but works on the west bank, said his commute now takes around two hours, including about half an hour spent walking across the Southern Bridge.
"We’ll have to walk like this every morning now. Taking a detour would take too long," Ihor, who declined to give his surname, told the Kyiv Independent.
Iryna was also crossing the bridge while it remained closed to traffic, but she was using an electric scooter to get across. Following the overnight attack on Oct. 27, this was her first time commuting to work this way.
"This is an alternative means of transport, but I don’t know how long the journey will take," Iryna, who also declined to give a surname, said, expressing hope that the bridge would be repaired soon.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that a university campus in the city was struck by Russia alongside Kyiv's well-known Kyoto park and residential buildings.
Education minister Andriy Butenko later said that the Russian attack damaged buildings and dormitories of the State University of Trade and Economics. He said there were no deaths among university students or employees.
"This is once again a terrorist country attacking educational institutions. A university, a scientific institution, a college, a school, or a kindergarten - the enemy directs its missiles at children, teachers, and scientists without any pity or humanity. There is no excuse for Moscow's cynical actions," Butenko added.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground first reported that loud explosions rocked the city in the Podilskyi and Obolonskyi districts at around 9:45 p.m. local time.
Just minutes earlier, Ukraine's Air Force warned that ballistic missiles and other missiles were headed toward Kyiv.
Explosions were heard near a metro station in Kyiv's Desnianskyi district, where a car was damaged, Klitschko reported .
Two medical facilities in the Dniprovskyi district were also damaged in the attack, Klitschko said. At one of the two sites that came under fire, blast waves shattered windows in the intensive care unit. Windows were also shattered at the other site.
A three-story commercial building was also "partially destroyed" in the district where one person was found dead, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) added.
A school building in the district was also damaged in the attack, the Kyiv City Military Administration wrote .
"Buildings of a university campus, dormitories, and nearby residential buildings were damaged" in the Desnyanskyi district, DSNS said .
Hours later, another wave of ballistic missiles attacked the city in the middle of the night.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported a new round of explosions at around 3:30 a.m. local time. At least seven explosions rocked the city in the space of three minutes. The blasts came minutes after Ukraine's Air Force warned that Russian ballistic missiles were bound for the capital.
Another blast shook Kyiv some 15 minutes later, without warning.
The second wave of missiles hit an administrative building in the Podilskyi district, Klitschko said . Non-residential buildings were also targeted in two other unspecified locations.
Some metro stations elsewhere in the city were damaged during the earlier attack, but were repaired by emergency workers overnight, the mayor reported.
Russia has attacked the Southern Bridge and other key bridges multiple times in October in an attempt to disrupt logistics and daily life in Kyiv.
Earlier in the night, Zelensky condemned Russia's attack on Kyiv and renewed calls for allies to provide Ukraine with air defense.
"Russian ballistic missiles struck the grounds of a university in Kyiv and the area around it — effectively the campus, Kyoto Park, the area near a metro station, and residential buildings," he said in a post to X.
"(I)t is precisely under such circumstances, when the threat is constant, when strikes can come at any moment and target cities and villages directly, that artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror," Zelensky added.
Russia regularly targets civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine as it continues to wage its war.
Ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a fatal Russian attack on the night of Oct. 13-14, killing five people and injuring another 25.
At least one person was killed, and 24 were injured in another Russian ballistic missile attack overnight on Oct. 22, during which cluster munitions also targeted the city.
Volodymyr Ivanyshyn is a news editor for The Kyiv Independent. He is pursuing an Honors Bachelor of Arts at the University of Toronto, majoring in political science with a minor in anthropology and human geography. Volodymyr holds a Certificate in Business Fundamentals from Rotman Commerce at the University of Toronto. He previously completed an internship with The Kyiv Independent.
"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," said Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
The highest number of casualties Ukrainian drones inflicted on the Russian military was recorded in March, with almost 34,000 soldiers killed or irrecoverably wounded.
Russia launched two waves of ballistic missiles at the capital overnight, targeting a major bridge, metro stations, and other civilian infrastructure.
Russian attacks hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge, disrupting metro services, as well as a university campus, an administrative building, and medical centers.
A ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid to enter the Russian occupied city began as Russian forces launched ballistic missiles at other parts of Ukraine.
Russia’s attacks on energy infrastructure, which weaponize winter to inflict suffering, amount to war crimes, a UN inquiry has found.
The attack is "part of a larger campaign of sabotage operations attributed to the Russian Federation in Europe," according to the Romanian Intelligence Service.
The investigation found that Russian designs for rocket-launched drones likely helped shape weapons China unveiled in 2025 and that Russian wind tunnels kept testing aircraft models for China's top arms maker after the invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Kyiv Ballistic Missile Strike Kills 1, Injures 15 in University Area and Multiple Districts
articles.title_zh: Kyiv Ballistic Missile Strike Kills 1, Injures 15 in University Area and Multiple Districts
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s university district, killing one person and injuring over 10, mostly students. Zelensky warned of further attacks and urged allies to accelerate air defense deliveries.
Russian ballistic missiles struck a university campus and surrounding residential areas in Kyiv late Monday, Oct. 26, killing at least one person and injuring over 10 others, most of them students, as emergency crews searched damaged buildings for people feared trapped under rubble.
The strikes hit the grounds of a university near Kyoto Park and Lisova metro station on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, damaging student dormitories, residential buildings, and medical facilities.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said nine of the wounded were hospitalized, including three in serious condition.
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that further strikes were possible as Russian Shahed drone attacks continued against the capital and other Ukrainian cities.
“There is extensive damage, and there are also reports that people may be trapped under the rubble,” Zelensky wrote on social media .
The Ukrainian leader stressed that the missiles struck crowded civilian areas where, he said, there were no military facilities nearby.
“Unfortunately, there may be more strikes coming,” Zelensky added.
At 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) reported that the number of casualties had risen to 15.
“Overnight, the enemy attacked the capital with ballistic missiles and [unmanned aerial vehicles] UAVs. As a result of the Russian Federation’s terrorist actions, damage has been recorded in three districts of Kyiv,” the report reads.
Of the 15 casualties, 12 have been hospitalized.
According to the State Emergency Service (DSNS), two fires broke out in non-residential buildings in the Obolonskyi district. Rescuers have extinguished both fires. Two casualties were reported in the district.
In the Holosiivskyi district, the Russian attack damaged transport infrastructure.
The university affected by the attack was identified as the State University of Trade and Economics (SUTE), located on Kyoto Street in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district.
The institution, founded in 1946, is one of the capital’s major public universities, with more than 15,000 students across six faculties, according to its official profile .
The university specializes in economics, international trade, finance, law, information technology, and management.
Russia’s ballistic strike landed near a university dormitory, shattering windows and injuring residents, according to Klitschko.
The mayor initially reported that a 20-year-old woman was hospitalized following the strike near the dormitory.
In a subsequent update , Klitschko said most of the 10 people injured in the attack were students living in university accommodation. Nine were taken to hospital.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported damage to university buildings, dormitories and nearby residential properties.
KMVA also reported damage to a school building in the Desnianskyi district.
A paramedic and an emergency medical technician suffered injuries after their ambulance came under fire in the Desnianskyi district, according to the mayor. Their injuries were not considered critical.
A strike near Lisova metro station also set a private vehicle on fire, while nearby residential infrastructure sustained damage.
In the Dniprovskyi district, a three-story non-residential building was partially destroyed, with emergency workers discovering the body of one person in its basement, according to the State Emergency Service.
The destruction extended across residential, educational and medical facilities in the two districts.
Zelensky renewed his call for faster deliveries of Western air defense systems and ammunition, warning that delays were leaving Ukrainian cities vulnerable to further Russian missile strikes.
He said Ukraine continued to face a constant threat from ballistic missiles that could strike populated areas with little warning.
Under such circumstances, he argued, “artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror.”
The president called for political agreements on defense assistance to be implemented promptly, stressing that Ukraine needed sufficient weapons not only to intercept incoming missiles but also to destroy Russian launchers.
The latest attack came amid an intensified Russian missile and drone campaign against Ukraine, with Kyiv’s residential neighborhoods, transport facilities, and civilian infrastructure repeatedly affected.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Modders unlock hidden AI performance on NVIDIA RTX 20, 30 and 40 series GPUs, with up to 2× tensor throughput
articles.title_zh: Modders unlock hidden AI performance on NVIDIA RTX 20, 30 and 40 series GPUs, with up to 2× tensor throughput
articles.content_orig:
Modders have found ways to remove NVIDIA’s compute performance restrictions on several generations of GeForce graphics cards. What started with the RTX 3090 series has now expanded to RTX 40 models and even the older RTX 2080 Ti.
The modifications can nearly double the throughput of certain Tensor Core operations without changing the hardware or flashing a new VBIOS. However, this does not mean twice the gaming performance, and the GeForce RTX 50 Blackwell series has yet to receive a confirmed working unlock.
The research builds on earlier attempts to unlock restricted compute capabilities on NVIDIA CMP mining GPUs. Developer Zagitta adapted these techniques for GeForce RTX 30 cards through the open-source GPU-Unlock project, while work involving TOTORONG’s firmware payload extended support to the Ada architecture.
Instead of modifying graphics drivers, the tools change low-level GPU configuration registers before the NVIDIA driver loads, removing limits on the rate at which certain Tensor Core instructions can be issued. The changes are temporary and are cleared when the GPU loses power.
The reported results are substantial in specific compute tests. An RTX 3090 Ti increased BF16 matrix multiplication performance from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS, while an RTX 4090 doubled its measured FP16 Tensor Core instruction throughput from 165.6 to 331.6 TFLOPS. KohakuBlueleaf has also demonstrated an RTX 2080 Ti reaching 111 TFLOPS, compared with 59.9 TFLOPS before the unlock. That particular card was already physically modified with 22GB of VRAM, which is unrelated to the software unlock. Successful tests have also been reported on RTX 3060, RTX 3070, RTX 3080 and selected RTX 40 models, although support is not yet validated across every GPU variant.
These modifications primarily affect FP16 and BF16 operations with FP32 accumulation, alongside certain TF32 and FP8 workloads on supported architectures. They can accelerate AI tasks involving matrix multiplication, including LLM prompt processing and some image-generation workloads.
However, actual gains depend on the software being used. RTX 3090 reports show LLM prompt-processing improvements of roughly 14% to 36%, while token generation remains largely unchanged because it is often limited by memory bandwidth. Gaming performance is unaffected by these specific unlocks. Most projects currently target Linux, although experimental Windows implementations are also available. They are not risk-free, and unsupported configurations may fail to boot.
Some users are already asking NVIDIA to officially remove these restrictions from older GeForce products, many of which are no longer manufactured. That would benefit owners using their existing GPUs for AI workloads, but it raises another question for gamers. Cards such as the RTX 3090 and RTX 4090 already attract AI buyers because of their 24GB memory capacity, and improving their compute performance could make them even more attractive on the second-hand market.
So perhaps asking NVIDIA to remove these restrictions is the right call, just not at the best time. It’s hard to argue against unlocking performance on GPUs that are no longer in production and, in most cases, already out of warranty. But the GPU market is hardly in good shape right now, and making older GeForce cards more attractive to AI users could make things even worse for gamers. But can it really get any worse?
Source: RTX 30 Unlock (GPU-Unlock), RTX 40 Unlock (GPU-Unlock-Ada), RTX 20 Unlock (Turing Unlock)

articles.title_orig: China’s First Distributed In-Hold Dredge Pump Equipped Ultra-Large Self-Propelled Dredger “Xin Hai Jing 1” Delivered
articles.title_zh: China’s First Distributed In-Hold Dredge Pump Equipped Ultra-Large Self-Propelled Dredger “Xin Hai Jing 1” Delivered
articles.content_orig:
It's on us. Share your news here.
Posted on October 27, 2026
On October 23, the “Xin Hai Jing 1,” China’s first extra-large self-propelled trailing suction hopper dredger designed with distributed in-hold dredge pumps, built by Shanghai Zhenhua Port Machinery (ZPMC) for CCCC Shanghai Dredging, was officially delivered at ZPMC Qidong Offshore Engineering base. The vessel achieves full-chain independent controllability of dredging equipment—from overall design to core components—and combines intelligent operation with green, low-carbon advantages. It will support major marine engineering projects and inject strong marine engineering momentum into the building of a maritime power.
It is reported that this vessel was constructed under a turnkey contract by the National Engineering Research Centre of Dredging and designed by the Marine Design and Research Institute of China (MARIC). With a maximum hopper capacity of 27,929 m³ and a maximum dredging depth of 120 meters, the vessel’s performance, environmental standards, and technical capabilities all rank among the world’s best, marking China’s achievement of full autonomy and control over the entire dredging equipment supply chain—from overall design to core components.
The “Xin Hai Jing 1” has an overall length of 180 meters, a beam of 36 meters, and a draft of 17.2 meters. Breaking away from the traditional centralized layout of mud pumps on cutter-suction dredgers, it is the first vessel to install two in-hold mud pumps in separate forward and aft pump compartments at the front and rear of the mud hold, respectively. This innovative hydrodynamic layout addresses the challenges of pipeline resistance and center of gravity balance in ultra-large vessels under extreme operating conditions, significantly enhancing stability and dredging efficiency under various loading conditions, and filling a gap in the design and application of distributed in-hold dredge pumps in China’s dredging industry.
Full-chain domestic production is the most outstanding achievement of the “Xin Hai Jing 1.” Centering on the requirements for ultra-large dredging depth, ultra-strong soil-breaking capability, and ultra-long discharge distance, all parties involved ine thconstruction adhered to demand-driven development and mobilized more than 110 domestic suppliers for collaborative research and development. Together they developed a series of core dredging-specific equipment, including a high-capacity, high-efficiency universal draghead suitable for both deep and shallow water, a lightweight 120-meter deep-water long drag arm system, and a high-efficiency hopper loading and overflow device. These efforts have driven a large number of core dredging-specific equipment items to complete domestic verification and supporting application, establishing a complete closed loop covering design and R&D, system integration, core supporting equipment, and full-scale ship verification, effectively shoring up shortcomings in China’s dredging and reclamation industry chain.
Intelligence and green development are the distinctive hallmarks of the “Xin Hai Jing 1.” The vessel is equipped with a new-generation intelligent monitoring and integrated management platform fully independently developed by China, adopting a “1 platform + N systems” architecture that enables fully automated control of “one-key dredging,” “one-key spoil dumping,” and “one-key reclamation,” and achieves “dredging-navigation integration” and even “unmanned dredging” under typical operating conditions.
Its digital twin system and “digital sentinels” based on AI vision and LiDAR can intelligently identify safety hazards such as smoke, flames, and oil leaks, with a recognition accuracy of over 95%. Both the main and auxiliary diesel engines are equipped with SCR denitrification systems. Through comprehensive measures including distributed in-hold dredge pumps, optimized pipeline layout, streamlined hull form for drag reduction, hybrid drive, and intelligent power and energy efficiency management, the vessel achieves a carbon emission reduction of more than 20% and a dredging efficiency improvement of approximately 30% compared with conventional vessels of the same type.
Once delivered and put into service, the vessel will be widely deployed for major projects such as deep-sea sand dredging, deep-water port and channel dredging along the coast, land reclamation, and coastal protection. It will further strengthen the capabilities of China’s ultra-large cutter suction dredger fleet and continue to advance the localization and iterative development of key supporting components, as well as the research and development of a series of related equipment.

articles.title_orig: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers
articles.title_zh: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers
articles.content_orig:
Suit that cites 2025 Guardian investigation alleges ‘pattern of inaccurate pricing’ that ‘affects millions of purchases’
The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states have sued Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, for persistently overcharging customers at its more than 20,000 stores across the United States.
The lawsuit , filed in federal court in Nashville, cites a Guardian investigation published last December.
“Dollar General has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve,” the 95-page legal complaint claims.
“Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country.”
The lawsuit says the scope of the retail chain’s “pricing misconduct” is “staggering”.
The FTC is the federal agency charged with protecting consumers from deceptive, unfair and anticompetitive business practices. State authorities from Mississippi to Ohio to Nebraska to Utah have joined the case as plaintiffs.
Dollar General pushed back against the allegations.
“The lawsuit filed today ... suggests that we have abandoned our mission and willfully disregarded the affordability needs of our customers,” the company said in statement . “Nothing could be further from the truth. Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store.”
The FTC’s allegations are consistent with the Guardian’s December 2025 investigation , which found that Dollar General stores failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period. That article “was the subject of significant internal deliberation and discussions” within the company, the lawsuit said.
The agency noted in the lawsuit that Dollar General has policies in place that are supposed to align register prices with shelf prices. For example, it directs employees to remove and replace outdated labels on certain days of the week. Workers told the Guardian that, because of understaffing, they are often too busy to change those labels.
“Dollar General’s on-paper policies to update pricing achieve little in practice,” the lawsuit said, because “they do not track whether the printed labels are actually affixed to shelves.”
The FTC cited a Guardian interview with a former lead sales associate in Louisiana who said: “I threw away tags sometimes, to keep me or a co-worker out of trouble.”
The lawsuit indicates that FTC investigators made undercover purchases at Dollar General stores in Ohio, Pennsylvania, Missouri and Maryland over a two and half month span. The first of these secret shopper tests took place this January, six weeks after the Guardian’s investigation focused wide attention on the discount chain’s pricing practices.
Every single undercover visit, the suit says, turned up overcharges on multiple products. At a Dollar General in Cleveland, eight of 58 items purchased rang up more costly than the prices listed on the product label or shelf – an overcharge rate of nearly 14%.
Dollar General said it first learned of the FTC’s investigation in February when it received a civil investigative demand from the agency. The company said that the investigation appeared to have “an unusually accelerated timeline” but that it “engaged cooperatively with the commission, producing more than 200,000 documents and over 350 gigabytes of data and making several company representatives available to provide sworn testimony on relatively short notice”.
The company’s statement said it pushed back against the calculations behind the FTC’s demand for financial compensation for consumers, but that it was surprised when the agency did not respond to its counteroffer and instead filed suit.
Dollar General said it “will defend this litigation vigorously”.
The company said that, in the retail marketplace, “occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement.”
In a separate case, the New York attorney general, Letitia James, announced earlier this month that Dollar General had agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it had repeatedly overcharged customers across the state.

articles.title_orig: From the Mediterranean to the dinner table
articles.title_zh: From the Mediterranean to the dinner table
articles.content_orig:
Bluefin tuna does not forgive delay. The fatty belly — otoro — is prized for a richness that seems to dissolve on the tongue, a quality built on gloss, deep color and a marine intensity that no cooked fish can replicate. That pleasure lasts only as long as the cold chain holds. A few hours of warmth, a break in handling, and the texture turns from silk to something far less forgiving.
Delivering bluefin at its best is therefore an industrial problem disguised as a culinary one. The fish must move from sea to ultra-low-temperature storage quickly, in volume, and without interruption.
The Ocean Star exists for that problem. It is a floating cold-chain hub that links Maltese harvesting expertise with Chinese cold-chain capacity.
It is an ultra-low-temperature processing and transportation vessel owned by Mediterranean Bluefin Industry Development (Hainan), a China-Malta joint venture specializing in bluefin tuna processing and trade.
The joint venture was established in June 2024 by Malta Fish Farming Ltd, or MFF, and China's Shandong Far-sea Development Ltd, covering trade, transportation and processing.
The vessel began a new production season in late September, operating in the Mediterranean east of Malta.
Workers weigh tuna on its decks, move product into refrigerated rooms, and dock at Valletta Port — images that trace the journey from harvest to cold storage.
MFF Chairman Salvu Ellul described the Ocean Star as the first ultra-low-temperature refrigerated transport and processing vessel and said it had become the most efficient bluefin tuna processing platform in the Mediterranean region.
He made the remarks on Oct 11 while briefing China's Ambassador to Malta, Zhang Zuo, during a visit to the Valletta waterfront in October.
Ellul told the ambassador that cooperation between the two nations in the fisheries sector had expanded year by year and that there were high expectations the partnership would serve as a bridge for economic and trade exchanges between China and Malta.
Ellul pointed to the Belt and Road Initiative as a source of trade opportunities, saying that Malta Fish Farming would ride the wind and waves to bring Malta's highest quality bluefin tuna products to the consumers' table worldwide.

articles.title_orig: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.title_zh: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.content_orig:
China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.
Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors , increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels.
The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.
Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.
That's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.
Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.
The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.
Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.
For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to.
On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.
David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China.
"The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.
The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week .
Europe isn't entirely without leverage.
The EU's new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.
It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.
Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.
Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.
Europe also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.
Fertmax FZCO's former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies.
"The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," he said.
For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.
Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.
Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.
Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics .
But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed.
The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.
Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.
However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.
Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.
Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.
However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.
A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes
articles.content_orig:
An extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.
Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters , according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems.
"While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.
In Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win.
Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.
"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."
Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.
In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition , a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system.
While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting.
Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats.
"Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot."
Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.
For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week.
What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.
After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
articles.content_orig:
The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty
When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.
As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.
The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption .
As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.
Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.
Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.
Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.
“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.
The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.
The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.
Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.
In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.
In January, Zhang Youxia , China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.
Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.
Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI says its AI model has disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis
articles.title_zh: OpenAI says its AI model has disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of computer science papers rest on a conjecture that an internal OpenAI model now claims to have refuted, the company said on Monday. OpenAI announced two more results the same day, one in mathematics and one in physics.
In a blog post , OpenAI said the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) has been “widely believed to be true”. The conjecture concerns how hard it is to solve Boolean satisfiability, a problem closely tied to P versus NP. Researchers have used it to show that problems in graph theory, computational biology, databases and other fields are hard to solve quickly.
According to OpenAI, its model found the disproof on 16 October. The company checked it in Lean, a language that verifies proofs by machine, the next day. It has published the model’s write-up and the Lean proof on GitHub.
A group led by Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego and Ryan Williams of MIT will check and explain the result. Impagliazzo and Paturi first proposed ETH with Francis Zane.
An internal model at OpenAI has produced a claimed refutation of ETH! Russell Impagliazzo, Mohan Paturi, and I have been asked to help organize an open and independent examination of this claim. 1/4
Ryan Williams @rrwilliams.bsky.social (@rrwilliams) October 26, 2026
In an open letter to their field, the three researchers said their role is not an endorsement.
“Our involvement should not be taken as certification of the claim. A result of this significance requires careful, independent scrutiny,” Impagliazzo, Paturi and Williams wrote.
Williams said on X that the group signed no non-disclosure agreements and will not be paid. The group asked OpenAI to release all its raw data on the ETH result and to fund a conference for the research community. OpenAI agreed to both, according to Williams and OpenAI.
In mathematics, OpenAI says its models proved the local smoothing conjecture, which Christopher Sogge proposed in 1991, in every dimension. That would also settle the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. Mathematicians had proved local smoothing in two dimensions in 2019 and the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions in 2025. OpenAI released the model’s write-up and a Lean proof, as it did with the 722 maths papers it published on 6 October.
In physics, OpenAI says its models produced a rigorous proof that certain quantum field theories exist in four dimensions. These include quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong force between quarks and gluons. The work includes a proof that pure Yang-Mills theory exists, which is part of one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize problems. OpenAI said in September it would not claim the prize for its Navier-Stokes proof .
Nobel laureate David Gross will lead the physics group, with Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov and Nikita Nekrasov. That group chose not to release the AI-produced material for now and will write up the work itself.
OpenAI says it does not seek academic credit for the discoveries. It says the researchers in each group should get the recognition for the explanations they write. It has also given $5m to the Simons Foundation for workshops and conferences on AI-produced results.
The three computer scientists ask in their letter how credit should work when AI finds results first. They warn that recognition may go to those who publish first or have the most powerful tools, while checking and explaining the work gets less credit. Mathematicians raised similar concerns in the Leiden declaration in June.
“If the claim is correct, it will change an important part of theoretical computer science,” the three researchers wrote.

articles.title_zh: US judge refuses to block Eli Lilly weight-loss drug ads, rules against Novo Nordisk
articles.content_orig:
A United States appeals court has ruled against the administration of President Donald Trump in its bid to block the state of California from counting certain mail-in ballots this election cycle.
In a decision on Monday, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request from the government to sequester roughly 20,000 mailed ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm election.
The Trump administration had asserted that the ballots were sent to people who are “likely” non-citizens.
But it has not publicly revealed how it created its list or determined that the voters identified upon it were ineligible due to their citizenship status.
In a two-to-one decision, the appeals court said the Trump administration had not given lower courts enough time to review the case. It therefore declined to stop California’s ballot tabulation.
The court’s majority also underscored that election administration was the state’s responsibility under the US Constitution.
The Trump administration was asking “the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain”, Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in his opinion.
Sanchez also warned that granting the Trump administration’s petition would be “inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The Trump administration filed its lawsuit against California on October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm vote on November 3.
California is a Democrat-led state, and Trump, a Republican leader, has repeatedly made unfounded claims that the state is prone to “cheating” in its elections.
The case is currently being weighed in a lower court, with a hearing scheduled for Tuesday.
But the Trump administration sought an expedited decision from the appeals court, pointing to the looming election date.
The midterm elections are critical to determine which political party holds power in Congress.
Currently, the Republican Party maintains slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, but experts project the Democratic Party is on track to make significant gains, flipping one or both chambers.
In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has raised the prospect of non-citizen voting as a threat to election integrity.
But experts say such voting is rare. California officials have likewise cast doubt on the administration’s claims of 20,000 ballots going to “likely non-citizens”, and they framed the administration’s lawsuit as an effort to interfere in the voting process.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing on October 20. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Trump’s Department of Justice has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for complete access to voter rolls that include sensitive personal data.
It has argued that releasing such information is necessary to prevent alleged voter fraud.
But the department has lost 26 of those cases thus far, with opponents successfully arguing that such manoeuvres could scare away voters and interfere with state election administration.
The Trump administration has yet to win any of the 30 cases.
Despite claims to the contrary by Trump and his allies, cases of illegal voting, including by non-citizens, are few and far between. Non-citizens are barred from participating in federal elections in all 50 states in the US.
In July, an investigation by the news service Reuters found only 129 cases of noncitizens being charged by federal authorities with illegal voting since 1996.
Many of those cases involved mistakes, like administrative errors or individuals being uncertain of voting rules, rather than fraudulent intent.
Voting rights advocates have also pointed to flaws in how the Trump administration has identified potential non-citizen voting, signalling some eligible voters may be disenfranchised as part of its efforts.
Immigration agents under Trump have been assigned to ferret out non-citizen voters, in some cases knocking on doors to inquire about the citizenship status of the residents inside.
Last week, the administration charged 28 immigrants in California with illegally voting.
But reporting from the Los Angeles Times found that some of the accused reacted to the charges with confusion and maintained that they never registered to vote.
Trump has a history of promoting false claims of election fraud in order to justify greater federal influence over the voting process.
In 2020, he lost his bid for re-election to Democrat Joe Biden, but he denied his defeat, instead blaming vote “rigging”. That claim prompted some of Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2023, in an apparent effort to halt the election certification.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market News, Oct. 26, 2026: Tech Shares Rally After Anthropic Files for Historic IPO
articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, Oct. 26, 2026: Tech Shares Rally After Anthropic Files for Historic IPO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
ORLANDO, Florida, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Stocks mostly rose on Monday, lifted by renewed optimism around AI as Anthropic filed for a US IPO and as investors awaited more 'Big Tech' earnings later this week. Weaker oil prices also support risk appetite.
The big exception, however, was Brazil, where financial assets plunged ‌following left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's shock win in Sunday's presidential election.
In my column today, I look at whether 'stagflation' pressures may be building in the US. ‌A deflating artificial intelligence bubble puts downward pressure on Wall Street and wider economic growth, but the revival of oil and energy prices is putting upward pressure on inflation. It's a tricky one for investors, and the ​Fed.
• Brazil stocks, real tumble as Lula win ends bullish run
• Anthropic's IPO filing shows explosive growth, risks and staggering costs
• Meta eyes record $95 billion equity raise to fund AI expansion
• In China, the AI bubble has already burst
• Fed to hit pause on rate hikes, but maybe not for long
• Today's Key Market Moves STOCKS: Brazil -14%. Asia mixed, Europe and UK up around 0.8%. Wall Street higher: Nasdaq +0.8%, S&P 500 +0.7%, Dow +0.3%.SECTORS/SHARES: Seven sectors on the S&P 500 rise, four fall. Tech +1.5%, comms services -1.4%. Tesla +5%, DoorDash -6%.FX: Brazilian real -8.5%, biggest fall since devaluation in 1999. Philippine peso sinks ‌to record low near 64.00/$. US dollar index edges higher.BONDS: ⁠Brazil buys back bonds, cancels auctions. US 2-year auction is ok — foreign demand dips, domestic demand surges.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil slips — Brent -0.8%, WTI -1.5%. Gold +0.5% back above $4,000/oz.
If investors were showing signs of AI fatigue in recent weeks, they're hiding it well as this week gets underway. On Monday, ⁠Anthropic filed for a US IPO, Meta announced plans for a $95 billion equity raise, and SpaceX said it has struck a $40 billion deal with Apollo Global Management for AI chip funding. The Anthropic IPO could value the company at a record-breaking $1.5 trillion or more, and Meta's capital raise would also be a record.
The eye-popping sums needed to fund the AI buildout have begun to suck some of the ​air ​out of the AI bubble, but that was shrugged off on Monday, at least temporarily — tech and AI ​stocks fueled a solid rebound on Wall Street. Competition for investor ‌capital is heating up.
Politically, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise election victory on Sunday was truly historic: never before had a candidate won the decisive second-round vote after losing the first. It also means a record-setting fourth term for Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday. Unsurprisingly, given the historic significance of Lula's comeback, there was a reaction across Brazilian markets.
Few doubt the scale of Brazil's fiscal and economic challenges, but Monday's collapse in Brazilian assets is likely to reverse, to some degree. Part of the selloff was because investors were caught so flat-footed. As late as Sunday, prediction markets were pointing to an 80% chance of a win for Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. But Lula's scope to push through an agenda that investors fear will ‌be limited, due to Bolsonaro's backing in Congress.
This week is one of the busiest in years ​for policymaking in the world's developed economies, with half of the G10 central banks set to decide interest ​rates. Monetary authorities in New Zealand and Canada are widely expected to hike by ​25 basis points, while those in the US, euro zone and Japan are expected to keep them on hold but signal possible increases in ‌December.
The common enemy is inflation, which is already too sticky in many ​countries. Oil and global energy prices remain elevated ​as war continues to choke Middle East supply routes, and the worry for policymakers is this bleeds into core inflation and becomes embedded in inflation expectations. But if the AI bubble deflates, growth, consumer confidence and investor sentiment could deflate too, putting policymakers in an even tighter bind.
What could move markets tomorrow?

• ​South Korea GDP (Q3, advance)
• US Treasury sells $70 billion of 5-year notes ‌at auction
• US durable goods (September)
• Corporate earnings, including Visa, Coca-Cola, Boeing, Seagate Technology, HSBC, Novartis

articles.content_orig:
The health of AI infrastructure businesses has been in question over the last few weeks, but that hasn't stopped banks from building out their AI infrastructure banking teams. Goldman Sachs just hired a senior banker from SMBC specialising in the financing arrangements for AI companies as the spotlight on firms like CoreWeave only gets brighter.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. 💥
Joseph Servi joined Goldman Sachs this month as a managing director in New York for AI infrastructure investment banking with a focus on data centres, GPUs and fiber optics. He spent the last two years at SMBC as co-head of its asset-backed securities (ABS) division as well as head of digital infrastructure and esoteric ABS origination. The role involved packaging the assets of AI infrastructure firms into securitized bonds or other products that are sold to investors. It's not clear exactly what his new role at Goldman will entail; the bank declined to comment.
Servi also previously worked in private equity as a principal with KKR working on structured capital markets for its digital infrastructure team.
Data centre ABS is a booming field; Barclays Research reported in July that outstanding issuance had grown to $61bn in 2026, up from $4bn in 2020. Some AI firms are instead using their assets as collateral for loans. CoreWeave raised $8.5bn earlier this year backed by its chips and a contract with Meta. As scrutiny of these firms increases, the need to package their financing arrangements well may become more important.
